levels.title: Symptoms, structure, or circumstance: separating what is experienced from what is explained

units.title: Distinguishing the experience, the adaptation, and the alternative explanation

lessons.title: Symptom or coping strategy: separating what a person experiences from what they do about it
lessons.explanation: Two different things are often collapsed into one word: an experience the person has, and an action the person takes. An intrusive thought, a wave of unbearable emotional distress, a sense of numbness, or a surge of agitation is something that happens to someone. Self-harm, heavy drinking, withdrawal from everyone, overworking, or rigid checking is something a person does, often in order to change how they feel. The NHS describes self-harm as, most often, a way to express or cope with emotional distress, and notes that not everyone who self-harms wants to end their life: some describe it as a way of staying alive by responding to severe distress.[1] That single distinction changes what you are being asked to explain. If you treat the behaviour as the disorder, you explain nothing; you merely rename the act. If you treat it as a solution, you immediately gain useful questions: solution to what, working how well, at what cost, and what would have to be available instead. Coping strategies are not irrational; they usually work in the short term, which is exactly why they persist. This lesson teaches you to hold the experience and the action apart, name the function, and stay honest about how much of that function you can actually infer. It is an educational reasoning exercise using fictional cases; it is not a method for diagnosing or treating yourself or anyone else.
lessons.example: A fictional person describes three things in one breath: 'I get thoughts that I am contaminated, I cannot settle until I have scrubbed my hands raw, and then I feel calm for about an hour.' The experience is the intrusive contamination thought together with the rising tension it produces. The behaviour is scrubbing. The reported consequence is roughly an hour of relief. Written as a chain it reads: trigger, intrusive thought and rising tension, scrubbing, brief relief, and then the thought returns. Everything after the relief is what maintains the pattern, because the act is the only thing that reliably lowers the tension. Now take a second fictional person who says, 'I drink two bottles of wine most nights. It started after my partner died. It is the only time I stop thinking about it.' The same three-part structure is present with different contents: an experience (grief and intrusive remembering), an action (drinking), and a function (hours of relief from thinking). Notice what the distinction does not tell you. It does not tell you whether this person has an alcohol use disorder, whether they also have a depressive episode, or what caused the grief. Those are separate questions with separate evidence requirements, and one of them, the alcohol question, is the subject of the next lesson.
lessons.question: A fictional client says: 'When the panic comes I pull out my hair. It is the only thing that stops the shaking.' Using the symptom/strategy distinction, what have you identified?
lessons.answer: An experience (panic and shaking) plus a behaviour with a stated short-term function (relief), which is not yet any diagnosis
lessons.distractor: A diagnosis of trichotillomania, because the behaviour is repetitive and the person cannot stop it
lessons.correction: A repetitive behaviour plus a stated function is a description, not a diagnosis. Naming the function generates questions about what the behaviour solves, what it costs, and what the person's own model of it is; it does not settle which, if any, category applies.

depth.definitions: A symptom is a subjective experience the person can report. A sign is something an observer can document. A coping strategy is a behaviour, deliberate or habitual, that a person uses to change an internal state or an external situation. Function is the consequence that maintains a behaviour; it is inferred from evidence, not read off the behaviour's form. Antecedent, behaviour, and consequence name the three parts of a functional analysis. Topography is what a behaviour looks like; function is what it does. Negative reinforcement means a behaviour is strengthened because it removes something aversive, which is why a strategy that reduces distress can become more frequent even as it becomes more harmful. Distinguish all of this from cause, which is a claim about origins, and from meaning, which is the person's own account of what the behaviour signifies. Nothing here requires the behaviour to be chosen, conscious, or pleasant.
depth.mechanism: The distinction matters because the two levels answer different questions and license different interventions. If the problem is framed as an experience, the questions concern its pattern, duration, impact, and differential. If it is framed as a strategy, the questions concern its trigger, its reliability, its costs, and the alternatives available in that person's actual life. Reading the NHS page on why people self-harm shows how many functions one behaviour can carry: a response to intrusive thoughts, a cry for help, relief of unbearable distress, self-punishment, an attempt to feel in control, or an attempt to express distress.[1] The same act, then, is not one thing. What follows is a practical rule: never accept a claim about function that is not attached to evidence. The evidence is usually a sequence. The person says the tension fell after the act; that is evidence for relief as one function. The person says they hid the injuries from everyone; that is evidence against communication as the dominant function in that instance, though it may be a function elsewhere. A second rule concerns the limits of the frame. Coping strategies can be maintained by negative reinforcement and yet also be attempts at communication, self-punishment, or control, all at once. Functions also change over time: the NHS page states plainly that the reasons can change and will not be the same for everybody.[1] So a functional formulation is a working hypothesis with a date on it, not a verdict.
depth.secondExample: The distinction can fail in both directions. Take a fictional student who stops attending lectures, sleeps most of the day, and no longer answers messages. It is tempting to read this as avoidance, that is, a coping strategy for social anxiety, and to design an exposure plan. But if the person also reports early waking, appetite loss, and a two-month inability to feel pleasure, the same observable behaviour is better explained as a symptom of a depressive episode, in which withdrawal is a consequence of reduced energy and reward rather than an attempt to manage anxiety. Now reverse it. Take a fictional man reported by staff as 'agitated and pacing, cannot sit still'. Observed only as a sign, this invites a category. But when he is asked, he describes a specific ritual he performs to stop intrusive images, and says pacing is the only way he has found to keep them at bay. The identical observable behaviour is now a coping strategy, and the assessment questions change completely. The transferable skill is the habit of asking what the behaviour is for before asking what the behaviour is, and holding the answer as a hypothesis to be tested against the person's own account and its consequences.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to treat the coping strategy as the disorder itself. Calling self-harm 'the problem' or a drinking pattern 'the problem' makes the behaviour the target and hides the distress it is managing, which is one reason people hide it. A second error is the mirror image: assuming every difficult or harmful behaviour must be a symptom of an illness and therefore a matter for medical explanation. Some coping strategies are learned, culturally normal, or simply effective at a cost. A third error is presuming function from form. Cutting and burning might look like different intentions, but the topography of an act tells you little about what it achieves for that person. A fourth, and the most corrosive, is the phrase 'attention-seeking', which is not an explanation but a way of closing inquiry; the same act is better described as communication, and communication is a legitimate function that deserves the same careful analysis as any other. Correct all four by writing down three columns: what the person reports experiencing, what you have observed, and what you are inferring about function, with the specific evidence for each inference attached.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Take these two fictional vignettes and produce a three-column table for each, headed Reported experience, Observed or reported behaviour, and Inferred function with evidence. Vignette A: 'I get a wave of dread in shops. I leave the trolley and walk out. Then I can breathe.' Vignette B: 'I get a wave of dread in shops. I stay, and I count products on the shelf until it fades. It takes about twenty minutes.' Then write one sentence for each naming a plausible alternative function of the same behaviour, and one sentence naming the single piece of new information that would change your mind. Model response for A: reported experience is dread in shops; behaviour is leaving; inferred function is escape or avoidance, evidenced by the reported relief on leaving; an alternative function is protecting a companion or a child from witnessing distress; the information that would change the mind is whether the dread reliably falls after leaving. Self-review rubric, four points: did you keep experience and action in separate columns; is every functional claim tied to a stated piece of evidence; did you offer at least one competing function; did you name the disconfirming observation rather than a vague 'more assessment'?
depth.summary: One sentence carries the lesson: separate what happens to a person from what a person does about it, then ask what the doing achieves and how you know. That habit converts a description into a set of answerable questions and protects you from two symmetrical errors, mistaking an act for an illness and mistaking an illness for a choice. It also sets up everything that follows in this unit: if behaviour has functions, then substances, developmental adaptations, and interpersonal patterns all need the same treatment, and the next lesson applies the frame to a group of causes that can imitate almost any psychiatric presentation.

readings.title: NHS, 'Why people self-harm' (sections: 'Some of the reasons that people may self-harm', 'Common causes of emotional distress', 'Self-harm and suicide')
readings.note: Read the bulleted list of reasons first and note that they are functions, not diagnoses: response to intrusive thoughts, a cry for help, relief of unbearable distress, self-punishment, control, communication. Then read 'Common causes of emotional distress' for the range of antecedents, and the 'Self-harm and suicide' subsection for the two statements this lesson relies on: that self-harm is most often described as a way to express or cope with distress, and that not everyone who self-harms wants to end their life. Public-facing NHS information, so read it as patient education rather than a clinical guideline.

readings.title: NICE NG225, Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (recommendations 1.1.1 and 1.14.2)
readings.note: In section 1.1 'Information and support', recommendation 1.1.1 lists what to discuss with someone who has self-harmed, beginning with 'what self-harm is' and then 'why people self-harm and, where possible, the specific circumstances of the person' - the guideline itself treats function as person-specific. Then read 1.14.2, which requires staff training to cover 'education about the underlying factors, triggers or motives that may lead people to self-harm'. NICE guidance is written for England; local pathways elsewhere differ.

visual.title: Two columns and a chain: experience, action, consequence
visual.description: A three-part instructional diagram that keeps an experience, a behaviour, and its consequence in separate labelled boxes, then shows how a competing explanation can be attached to the same observable behaviour.
steps: Left column, headed Experience: place only what the person reports or what an observer documents - intrusive thoughts, dread, numbness, agitation.
Centre column, headed Action: place only what is done - scrubbing, drinking, leaving the shop, pacing, cutting.
Right column, headed Consequence and evidence: write the reported change after the action and mark whether it was the person's report, an observation, or your inference.
Draw a feedback arrow from Consequence back to Action, labelled 'relief maintains the behaviour', and note that this is negative reinforcement and not a claim about choice.
Below, add a second row for the same Action with a different Experience box attached, to show that identical behaviour can carry a different formulation.
Finally, mark one box with a dotted outline and the label 'evidence needed', to represent the single observation that would change the formulation.

lessons.title: Substance use, intoxication, and withdrawal as diagnostic confounders
lessons.explanation: Substances are the most efficient mimics in psychiatry. Intoxication and withdrawal can produce low mood, elevated mood, anxiety, panic, paranoia, hallucinations, disorientation, agitation, insomnia, and cognitive change, and the person may present at any point in that sequence. The clinical question is almost never 'is a substance involved?' but 'is what I am seeing the direct effect of use or withdrawal, an independent condition that coexists with use, or a condition that use has been recruited to manage?' Those three answers require different evidence. Timing is the most useful single lever: symptoms that appear only in a window around use or cessation, and that resolve with sustained abstinence, are more likely substance-induced, while a symptom pattern with its own onset, duration and course outside that window is less easily explained away. There is no shortcut that settles this from a single conversation. This lesson is education about clinical reasoning, using fictional cases; it is not advice about any person's substance use, and it contains no dose, taper, or treatment instruction.
lessons.example: A fictional person is brought to an emergency department on the fourth day after stopping a long-standing heavy drinking pattern. They are feverish, sweating, agitated, disoriented as to where they are, and report seeing insects on the wall while their heart rate is high. A colleague writes 'first episode of psychosis' on the notes. Walk through the correction. The published description of alcohol withdrawal syndrome in StatPearls states that the syndrome typically begins with mild anxiety, headache, gastrointestinal discomfort and insomnia, may progress to alcohol hallucinosis with visual or auditory hallucinations that usually subside within 48 hours of cessation, that withdrawal seizures may occur within hours, and that alcohol withdrawal delirium - formerly called delirium tremens, with fever, tachycardia, agitation, diaphoresis, hallucinations, disorientation and hypertension - is the most severe form and may appear anywhere from three to eight days after cessation.[1] The published estimate given there is that roughly three to five per cent of people with alcohol withdrawal syndrome progress to withdrawal delirium, and that it may be fatal. The disorientation, the fever, the autonomic signs and the day-four timing are not the features of a first psychotic episode; they are the features of a medical emergency. The lesson is not that colleagues should memorise one syndrome. It is that a presentation the observer has cast as psychiatric was, on the timeline alone, a presentation that required a different pathway first.
lessons.question: A fictional patient is described as anxious, tremulous and sleepless, with symptoms beginning about ten hours after their last drink and easing over the following days. What does this pattern most strongly suggest?
lessons.answer: A withdrawal-state explanation should be considered first, and the presentation reassessed after a period of observed abstinence
lessons.distractor: An anxiety disorder, because anxiety and insomnia are the presenting features and the person is not confused
lessons.correction: The presenting features are non-specific and appear in both explanations, which is exactly why the timeline is the discriminating evidence. Onset within hours of cessation and resolution with abstinence point to a withdrawal state; a diagnosis of an anxiety disorder would need a pattern with its own course outside that window.

depth.definitions: Intoxication is the acute effect of a substance. Tolerance is a reduced response after repeated use. Withdrawal is a syndrome produced by reduction or cessation after a period of use; it requires neuroadaptation, not merely use. A substance-induced disorder is a syndrome whose features arise in the context of use or withdrawal and resolve with abstinence. Coexisting disorder, sometimes called dual diagnosis, means a psychiatric condition that persists independently of use. Kindling is the published observation that successive withdrawal episodes tend to be more severe, especially with respect to seizure risk. The CIWA-Ar is a severity scale for alcohol withdrawal described in StatPearls, in which a score of eight or less is described as mild, between eight and fifteen as moderate, and above fifteen as severe. Delirium is a disturbance of attention and awareness with an acute onset and fluctuating course; it is a medical syndrome, not a mood state.
depth.mechanism: The reason substances confound psychiatric assessment is that the same output can arrive through several routes. A person may use a substance because of pre-existing distress, may develop distress as a consequence of use, or both, and the published NIMH patient-facing page sets out exactly this three-way possibility: shared environmental contributors such as stress or trauma and genetics, mental disorders raising the risk of substance use partly as coping, and substance use producing brain changes that raise the risk of other mental disorders.[3] Order of onset is evidence about which route is more likely, but it is weak evidence; people's recall of first use and first low mood is approximate. Withdrawal adds a second layer of difficulty because it is a moving target. StatPearls describes the standard explanatory model as neuroadaptation in inhibitory and excitatory signalling, with the balance shifting during chronic use and then producing an excitatory state when the substance is removed, and it also documents the kindling observation.[1] That model is a useful organising description of the syndrome, not a licence to explain any individual person's presentation from a single transmitter story; the same page goes on to describe a clinical assessment based on history, physical findings and severity scales rather than on any biochemical test. Two honest limitations close the loop. First, severity scales exist and can be used to track change, but a score is not a diagnosis and does not replace examination. Second, the public health picture is uneven: the WHO fact sheet records roughly 400 million people aged fifteen or older living with alcohol use disorders and about 209 million with alcohol dependence in the 2019 data, and states that access to treatment remains very low, with the proportion of people with alcohol use disorders in contact with treatment services varying from under one per cent to no more than fourteen per cent.[2] Prevalence figures of that kind describe populations; they must never be used as a reason to assume an individual's explanation.
depth.secondExample: Now take a fictional person in their twenties brought in by friends, agitated, suspicious and talking rapidly after several days of heavy stimulant use. The easy reading is 'substance-induced psychosis', and the timeline supports it, since the features began in the context of use. But the case turns on two extra pieces of information. First, did any of this predate the substance use? The person's partner says there were two weeks of withdrawal and unusual beliefs about neighbours two months earlier, before the current pattern of use began. Second, what happens over the next days with observed abstinence? The published NIMH page stresses that symptoms may overlap and that assessment by clinicians experienced in both problems is what reduces the chance of a missed diagnosis.[3] The reverse scenario is equally common and equally misleading. A fictional person starts drinking heavily only after a bereavement, at the same time as low mood and sleeplessness. Here the substance is more plausibly a response to the mood state than its cause. The same two questions decide it: order of onset relative to symptoms, and what remains after a sustained period without the substance. Note that neither question produces certainty from a single interview. Both produce a working hypothesis with a named test.
depth.mistake: The first error is diagnostic overshadowing in the substance direction: once a substance is identified, every feature is attributed to it, and the person's own report of long-standing symptoms is discounted. The second error is the mirror image, a failure to consider substances at all, so that a treatable withdrawal state is managed as an anxiety or sleep problem. A third error is treating a severity score as a diagnosis rather than as a repeated measure, which encourages the idea that the underlying problem has been identified. A fourth is inferring causality from co-occurrence, so that the mere presence of use is taken to mean the use is the cause. The correction is procedural rather than conceptual: write the timeline explicitly, with the dates of first use, last use, and symptom onset, then state which of the three explanations the timeline supports and what observation over the next days would discriminate. If you cannot write the timeline from the information you have, that absence is itself the finding to record. The NICE guideline on coexisting severe mental illness and substance misuse adds a further correction in its recommendations for first contact, where it directs staff to look out for multiple needs including physical health problems and unstable housing, and to remember that people may struggle to access services because they face stigma.[4]
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Build a timeline for this fictional case on one page and write a three-line conclusion. The case: a 34-year-old is admitted with agitation, poor sleep, and beliefs that neighbours are monitoring them. Heavy drinking is reported, most recently stopping two days ago. They disclose three weeks of low mood and sleeplessness beginning when they lost their job, and say they had similar beliefs for a few days once before, aged 26, during a period of heavy use that stopped. Model response: the timeline runs job loss, then low mood and sleeplessness, then heavy drinking, then last drink, then agitation and unusual beliefs two days into cessation. The three-line conclusion should say which features are most likely substance- or withdrawal-related, which could persist independently of use, and the single observation that would most change the answer, for example whether the unusual beliefs and low mood persist after two to three weeks without alcohol and with sleep restored. Self-review rubric, four points: are first use, last use and symptom onset all dated; is each attribution linked to a specific timeline feature rather than to a general impression; is at least one feature left deliberately unresolved; and does the disconfirming observation concern the person's course over time rather than a test result you would need equipment to obtain?
depth.summary: Substances sit at the junction of every other topic in this level, which is why they are treated early. The discipline is to separate three claims - present, causing, and coexisting - and to test them against a timeline rather than an impression. Order of onset offers a hypothesis; sustained abstinence over an observed interval is the sharper evidence. When you cannot obtain either, the honest output is a provisional formulation and a stated plan for reassessment, a pattern the next lesson repeats in a developmental key.

readings.title: StatPearls, Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome (sections: Introduction, Epidemiology, Pathophysiology, History and Physical, Evaluation)
readings.note: Read the Introduction and History and Physical sections for the timeline this lesson uses: symptoms may begin within hours and peak around 72 hours, seizures can occur within hours, hallucinosis usually subsides within 48 hours, and alcohol withdrawal delirium may occur anywhere from 3 to 8 days after cessation with an estimated 3 to 5 per cent of people with withdrawal progressing to it. Then read Pathophysiology for the adaptation-and-kindling account and Evaluation for the CIWA-Ar severity bands and the point that the CIWA-Ar cannot be used in a patient who is not alert. StatPearls is written for clinicians as a study resource and is not a substitute for a guideline; some hosts intermittently present a verification step to automated requests.

readings.title: WHO, Alcohol fact sheet (Key facts, Overview, Health risks of alcohol use, Factors affecting alcohol consumption)
readings.note: Use the Key facts box for the population figures quoted in this lesson: approximately 2.6 million deaths attributable to alcohol in 2019, about 400 million people aged 15 and older living with alcohol use disorders, and about 209 million with dependence. Then read the paragraph in Overview on access to treatment, which states that the proportion of people with alcohol use disorders in contact with treatment services varies from less than 1 per cent to no more than 14 per cent. The Fact sheet is a global public-health summary, not clinical guidance, and its figures are dated to 2019.

readings.title: NIMH, Finding Help for Co-Occurring Substance Use and Mental Disorders (sections: 'Why do substance use and other mental disorders occur together?' and 'How are these co-occurring disorders diagnosed and treated?')
readings.note: This page sets out the three routes this lesson teaches: shared environmental and genetic contributors, mental disorders raising the risk of use including use as coping, and substance use contributing brain changes that raise the risk of other mental disorders. It also states that accurate diagnosis matters because symptoms may overlap. Written for the public, so treat the causal discussion as a summary of research possibilities rather than a settled mechanism.

readings.title: NICE NG58, Coexisting severe mental illness and substance misuse (recommendations 1.1.1 and 1.1.2)
readings.note: Read section 1.1 'First contact with services'. Recommendation 1.1.1 directs staff to look out for multiple needs including physical health problems and unstable housing, and notes that people may find services hard to access because they face stigma. Recommendation 1.1.2 lists chronic physical health conditions to be aware of, including cardiovascular, respiratory and hepatic complications. Note that NG58 covers community health and social care services and is written for England.

visual.title: Timeline with three attribution lanes
visual.description: A horizontal timeline with dated markers, placed above three labelled lanes that show how the same symptoms can be attributed to intoxication, withdrawal, or an independent condition.
steps: Draw the time axis and mark four events in order: first use, symptom onset, last use, and presentation.
Draw lane one, headed Substance effect, and shade the intervals where ongoing use could plausibly produce the symptoms.

Draw lane two, headed Withdrawal effect, and mark the interval that begins at last use: hours for tremor and seizures, around 72 hours for peak severity, and days three to eight for the risk of withdrawal delirium.
Draw lane three, headed Independent condition, and mark a bracket that extends on both sides of the substance interval, labelled 'would need to persist beyond observed abstinence'.
Place each reported symptom as a dot in whichever lane or lanes the timeline supports, and leave any symptom that fits more than one lane straddling the boundary.
Add a footer line reading 'order of onset is evidence, not proof', and one arrow labelled 'reassess after abstinence' pointing past the last dated marker.

lessons.title: Neurodevelopmental presentations across the lifespan
lessons.explanation: Neurodevelopmental conditions are present from early development, but the reason someone comes to attention is usually not the condition itself. It is the point at which the demands of their environment outrun the support available. That is why autism and ADHD can be identified in childhood in one person and in midlife in another, and why the same underlying profile can look entirely different at five, fifteen and fifty. The WHO states that characteristics of autism may be detected in early childhood but that autism is often not diagnosed until much later, and that abilities and needs vary and can evolve over time.[1] NICE guidance for autistic adults asks professionals to understand the nature, development and course of autism, its impact on personal, social, educational and occupational functioning, the impact of the environment, and what it calls the potential discrepancy between intellectual functioning measured by IQ and adaptive functioning in daily life.[2] Those four items are effectively a specification for a lifespan assessment. The clinical skill in this lesson is to build a developmental history that tracks a person's profile against changing demands, rather than asking whether they 'really' have it. The material is education about assessment reasoning; it is not a means of diagnosing anyone, and it contains no treatment or medication instruction.
lessons.example: A fictional woman is referred at 39 after her son's assessment. Reading the referral tells you almost nothing, so the assessment builds a table across time. Primary school: no friendships, strong fairness rules, distress at timetable changes, and a report that she was 'quiet but fine'. Secondary school: academic success, exhaustion at the end of each day, and copying classmates to work out what to say. University: one intense friendship, one severe burnout episode. Work: exceptional output on defined tasks, repeated conflict when plans changed, two jobs left after restructuring. Home: rigid routines and a need for planned downtime that she had never described to anyone because it seemed ordinary. Note what the pattern shows. Nothing appeared at 39; the ratio of demand to support changed. NICE guidance for identifying possible autism in adults directs staff to consider assessment where there are persistent difficulties in social interaction or communication, or rigid and repetitive behaviour, resistance to change or restricted interests, together with at least one of: problems obtaining or sustaining employment or education, difficulties initiating or sustaining social relationships, previous or current contact with mental health or learning disability services, or a history of a neurodevelopmental condition or mental disorder.[2] Now contrast the same-shaped referral for someone whose concentration and social difficulties began eighteen months ago after a bereavement. Childhood onset in a pattern that pervades settings is the feature that distinguishes the two, and lifelong difficulty is not demonstrated, it is established by history.
lessons.question: Two fictional adults are referred for concentration problems. One describes the same difficulties at primary school, at university and in three jobs, and a sibling with the same profile. The other describes them beginning after a recent illness. What does the developmental history contribute?
lessons.answer: It establishes whether the pattern is lifelong and pervasive across settings, which changes the candidate explanations rather than settling the diagnosis
lessons.distractor: It confirms the diagnosis, because lifelong difficulties are the defining feature of a neurodevelopmental condition
lessons.correction: A lifelong, cross-setting pattern raises the likelihood that a neurodevelopmental profile should be considered and makes a recently acquired explanation less adequate. It is not sufficient on its own: current impairment, alternative explanations such as mood, sleep and substance effects, and the impact on daily functioning all still have to be assessed.

depth.definitions: Neurodevelopment refers to the processes by which the nervous system develops, and neurodevelopmental conditions are those in which development differs in a way that affects interaction, communication, learning, attention or movement. Autism is described by the WHO as a diverse group of conditions characterised by some degree of difficulty with social interaction and communication and by atypical patterns of activities and behaviours, including difficulty with transitions, a focus on details, and unusual reactions to sensations.[1] ADHD refers to persistent patterns of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity that cause impairment. Masking, also called camouflaging, means deliberately or automatically suppressing or compensating for features in order to fit a setting. A developmental history is a timeline of first concerns, supports, and functioning across settings. An informant is someone who can describe the person's earlier functioning. Adaptive functioning is the ability to manage everyday tasks, which NICE notes may diverge from measured IQ. Under-recognition means that a condition is present but not identified.
depth.mechanism: Why does the surface presentation change so much across the lifespan? Four mechanisms do most of the work. First, demand rises: a person's difficulties become visible when the environment requires more social inference, more organisation, or more flexibility than their current strategies can supply. Second, scaffolding falls away: school timetables, parental routines and structured employment secretly carry a great deal of executive and social load, and their removal is often the event that prompts a referral. Third, compensatory effort is finite. Masking is effortful, and its cost typically appears later as exhaustion, anxiety or depression rather than as the original feature, so a clinician who assesses only the surface may see a mood disorder and stop there. Fourth, referral patterns are uneven. NICE's ADHD guideline recommends considering the diagnosis in adults who have a mental health condition, a history of substance misuse, or another neurodevelopmental disorder, which is a direct statement that these presentations arrive disguised.[3] The WHO adds an important caution about figures: the global estimate is about 1 in 127 people in 2021, but reported prevalence varies substantially across studies, some well-controlled studies report substantially higher figures, and prevalence in many low- and middle-income countries is unknown.[1] Those uncertainties are about populations. They do not tell you anything about the person in front of you, and a prevalence figure can never function as a diagnostic threshold. One further point deserves care: the same WHO page devotes an entire section to the repeatedly tested finding that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine does not cause autism, and records that the original paper was withdrawn and its author lost his medical licence.[1] Any framing that implies otherwise is contradicted by the source.
depth.secondExample: Take a fictional man of 71, referred after his wife's death because his daughter finds him 'inflexible and unable to cope'. His history: the same fixed daily order for forty years, a career in a technical field with exceptional attention to detail, two friends, and distress at unplanned changes for as long as anyone can remember. There is no deterioration from a baseline; there is a baseline, and the baseline lost its scaffolding when his wife died. Compare that with a fictional man of the same age whose changes began eight months ago: he now repeats questions, gets lost on a familiar route, and has stopped managing his own medication. Same age, same family complaint, opposite significance. The first pattern is consistent and long-standing; the second is a change from a previously higher level of function and needs a different assessment pathway. This is the same reasoning the earlier level applied to acute change, transposed into a developmental key. It also shows why asking a person whether they 'have always been like this' is not enough on its own: the person may have had nothing to compare against, and may have constructed an entire life around accommodating a profile they never had a name for.
depth.mistake: The first error is the belief that autism or ADHD is a childhood diagnosis that cannot be made in adults. The sources contradict it directly: the WHO records that autism is often not diagnosed until much later than early childhood,[1] and NICE's ADHD guideline addresses adult services, adult recognition and adults with coexisting mental health conditions and substance use.[3] The second error is the opposite over-extension, treating the labels as explaining everything, so that every difficulty in a person's life becomes a symptom. A third error is to treat an adult diagnosis as evidence that the presentation is mild, when identification in adulthood often reflects high compensatory effort rather than low impact. A fourth is deficit framing, which locates the problem entirely inside the person; NICE explicitly asks staff to consider the physical environment, personal space, lighting and noise, and to make adjustments where the environment is a factor.[2] Correct the first three by writing the developmental timeline with dates and settings, and by keeping the profile, the current state, and the environment in separate columns. Correct the fourth by asking what has changed in the environment whenever you are tempted to describe the person as having become worse.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Build a five-column lifespan table for this fictional case and write a two-sentence conclusion. Columns: age band, setting, what was difficult, what support was carrying the load, and what was said about it at the time. The case: a 27-year-old refers himself. He describes needing hours alone after work, a long-standing inability to tell when a conversation has turned hostile, intense focus on one topic, and repeated sick leave for exhaustion. He says school was 'fine, I was just quiet', that his mother organised everything until he moved out at 22, and that his only close friendship ended when he could not tell what he had done wrong. Model response: the table should show support falling away around 22 while demands rose, with exhaustion appearing as the presenting feature rather than as the original difficulty; the two-sentence conclusion should state that a developmental pattern should be assessed across settings rather than inferred from the current presentation, and should name the alternative explanations that still need excluding. Self-review rubric, four points: does every row carry a setting as well as an age; is the disappearance of an earlier support recorded explicitly; are the person's own words used rather than replaced with your paraphrase; and does the conclusion state what remains unknown instead of implying a settled answer?
depth.summary: Neurodevelopmental assessment is longitudinal by nature. The questions are not whether a person has a condition but when the profile was first observable, in which settings it is present, what currently carries the load, and what the environment is doing to the presentation. Demand, scaffolding, compensatory effort and referral bias explain most of the apparent change across the lifespan, and prevalence estimates are too imprecise to function as thresholds. The next lesson takes up the related problem of what to do with a stable pattern of traits in someone whose difficulties are real but whose pattern does not look like an episode at all.

readings.title: WHO, Autism fact sheet (Key facts, Overview, Epidemiology, Causes, Assessment and care, Human rights)
readings.note: Take the Key facts box first: autism is a diverse group of conditions related to development of the brain; characteristics may be detected in early childhood but autism is often not diagnosed until much later; abilities and needs vary and can evolve. Then read Epidemiology for the 2021 estimate of about 1 in 127 people and the statement that reported prevalence varies substantially and is unknown in many low- and middle-income countries. Read Causes for the vaccine section, which states that extensive research has demonstrated that the MMR vaccine does not cause autism and that the study suggesting a link was withdrawn and its author struck off. Public-health summary, not clinical guidance.

readings.title: NICE CG142, Autism spectrum disorder in adults (recommendations 1.1.2, 1.1.3, 1.1.5, 1.1.8 and 1.2.2)
readings.note: Recommendations 1.1.2 and 1.1.3 list what staff should understand, including the nature, development and course of autism, its impact on functioning, the impact of the social and physical environment, and the potential discrepancy between measured intellectual functioning and adaptive functioning. Recommendation 1.1.5 concerns communication support and addressing the person using the name and title they prefer. Recommendation 1.1.8 is about adjusting the physical environment: personal space, visual supports, low-arousal colours, reduced fluorescent lighting, noise reduction. Recommendation 1.2.2 sets out the circumstances in which to consider assessment for possible autism in an adult. Written for England, and the terminology reflects the guideline's publication date.

readings.title: NICE NG87, Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (recommendations 1.1.1, 1.1.2 and 1.2.1)
readings.note: Read section 1.1 for the statement that people with ADHD would benefit from better integration of child, adolescent and adult mental health services and separate specialist teams for adults, and the requirement for information-sharing arrangements covering transition. Then read the recognition recommendation begin at 1.2.1, which lists groups in whom ADHD should be considered, including people with other neurodevelopmental disorders, adults with a mental health condition, and people with a history of substance misuse. The guideline is for England; this lesson uses only its recognition and service-arrangement logic and none of its medication content.

visual.title: Lifespan demand curve against a flat support line
visual.description: A line graph with age on the horizontal axis, showing rising environmental demand and a support line that steps down at life transitions, with the gap between them shaded as the point of presentation.
steps: Draw the age axis from 5 to 70 and plot a rising line labelled Environmental demand, with visible steps at school entry, secondary school, leaving home, and employment change.
Plot a second line labelled Available support and scaffolding, stepping downward at the same transitions.
Shade the widening region between the two lines and label it 'gap where difficulty becomes visible'.
Place markers along the shaded region naming what appears there: exhaustion, anxiety, missed deadlines, conflict after restructuring.
On a second panel, redraw the same axes for a profile acquired recently, with demand flat and a single sharp step in required function, labelled 'change from baseline'.
Add a caption distinguishing the two: one shows a long-standing profile meeting a new demand, the other shows a change from a previously established level.

lessons.title: Personality structure versus personality disorder
lessons.explanation: Everyone has a personality in the ordinary sense: a stable-ish pattern of thinking, feeling and relating. A personality disorder is a different kind of claim. It asserts that such a pattern is pervasive and inflexible, that it produces significant distress or impairment across contexts, and that it is traceable to adolescence or early adulthood rather than appearing as an episode. The Royal College of Psychiatrists describes the diagnosis as applying to people whose traits make it extremely difficult to manage their emotions and feelings about themselves, others and the world, and who have significant problems coping day to day and in their relationships, and it adds a sentence that should be read first rather than last: being told you have a 'disordered' personality can be upsetting and hurtful, but it does not mean there is something wrong with who you are.[1] The classification has also moved. Until 2019 the diagnosis was split into ten categories; RCPsych states that some of those category names are now considered stigmatising, and that personality disorder is now organised by severity together with one or more of five trait domains - negative affectivity, detachment, dissociality, disinhibition, and anankastia.[1] This lesson teaches you to separate three things that get muddled: a description of traits, a claim about a threshold being crossed, and an explanation of the present episode. It is education about diagnostic reasoning with fictional examples, not a means of assessing anyone.
lessons.example: A fictional person is described by a friend as 'the most intense person I know - she either loves you completely or cuts you off'. That is a trait description. Now add the things that would be needed before any threshold claim. Is the pattern pervasive, appearing in work, family and friendships, or is it concentrated in intimate relationships? When did it start: is there a report of this at fifteen, or did it begin in the last year? What is the impact: recurrent job losses, ruptures, or self-harm episodes, and does the person experience it as distressing? What else could account for it: a current mood episode, an active substance pattern, a trauma response, or a reaction to a genuinely unsafe situation? Notice that none of these questions is answered by the friend's description, and each of them can be answered by evidence of a different kind. Now the second move. Suppose the pattern is lifelong, pervasive and impairing. Does that make it the explanation for today's crisis? No. StatPearls describes how clinicians must recognise countertransference, which can negatively affect patient care, and suggests using the clinicians' own feelings as an evaluation tool to guide assessment.[2] That is a useful discipline: the pull to describe someone in evaluative terms is itself data about the interaction, and it is not a diagnostic finding.
lessons.question: A fictional client is described by a colleague as 'borderline' after two difficult appointments in which he was angry and then tearful. He has been in services for three months following a bereavement. What is the strongest correction?
lessons.answer: The description is a reaction to a recent episode; a threshold claim would require a pervasive, long-standing pattern plus distress or impairment across contexts, which has not been assessed
lessons.distractor: The label is clinically justified because intense anger alternating with tearfulness is the pattern the category describes
lessons.correction: Alternating anger and tearfulness is compatible with grief, a mood episode, a substance effect, or a reaction to a service. The category requires pervasiveness and a course beginning in adolescence or early adulthood, and the three-month history actively weighs against that.

depth.definitions: Personality is the characteristic pattern of thinking, feeling and relating that makes a person recognisable across situations. A trait is one dimension of that pattern. Temperament refers to early-appearing, biologically influenced dispositions. A disorder, in this context, is a threshold claim: the pattern must be pervasive and inflexible, must cause clinically significant distress or impairment, and must be evident from adolescence or early adulthood, with the pattern not better explained by another condition. RCPsych also lists 'personality difficulty', which is explicitly not a diagnosis of personality disorder, and a severity ladder running mild, moderate and severe, where severe is described as serious challenges across all areas of life.[1] Dimensional classification rates severity and describes traits rather than sorting people into types; categorical classification assigns a named type. Egodystonic means the person experiences the pattern as foreign and unwanted; egosyntonic means it fits how they see themselves. Countertransference is the clinician's emotional reaction to the patient, and it distorts judgement if it is not noticed.
depth.mechanism: Why is the threshold so contested? Start with the definition itself. StatPearls gives the DSM-5-TR formulation as an enduring pattern of inner experience and behaviour that deviates significantly from the norms and expectations of the surrounding culture, is pervasive and inflexible, generally starts in adolescence, persists through adulthood, and causes distress or impairment.[2] Two clauses in that sentence do a lot of quiet work. 'Deviates from the norms and expectations of the surrounding culture' makes the judgement partly cultural, so what counts as disordered shifts as norms shift. 'Enduring' implies stability, and the evidence is more mixed than the word suggests: StatPearls records that in people with antisocial personality disorder who achieve remission the mean age is 35 and that remission is predicted by less baseline symptomatology,[2] and the RCPsych page has a section titled 'Do people with a personality disorder diagnosis get better?' written specifically to counter the misconception that they do not, followed by a section on what happens without help.[1] Second, the diagnostic act is interpersonal. Assessment happens in relationships, often under strain, often in crisis, and the clinician's own reactions - frustration, protectiveness, a wish to end the appointment - are exactly the conditions in which a stable trait label is easiest to apply and hardest to revise. Third, prevalence estimates illustrate how provisional the numbers are. StatPearls states that the World Health Organization has estimated the prevalence of having a personality disorder at 6.1 per cent, and gives separate estimates for the three clusters of 3.6, 1.5 and 2.7 per cent - which sum to 7.8 per cent, more than the overall figure quoted beside them. That excess is not a scandal; it is a reminder that these are estimates drawn from different sources and study designs rather than a reconciled ledger, and that no single published number should be treated as precise. Fifth, the label is sticky in a way that an episode label is not, because it is recorded as a feature of the person rather than of a period of their life.
depth.secondExample: Both symmetrical errors are easy to make, and both are avoided by the same three columns. Take a fictional person whose traits are strong, stable and impairing only to herself: she is extremely orderly, cannot delegate, and becomes distressed when plans change. Colleagues regard her as rigorous; she has had two episodes of exhaustion requiring leave. There is no requirement that a trait pattern be harmful to others, and no requirement of crisis; the question is pervasiveness, duration and clinically significant distress or impairment. Now take a fictional young man with repeated emergency presentations after arguments, a long history of disrupted schooling from age thirteen, contact with services since fifteen, and a current episode of low mood. Here the developmental course is available and the pattern is pervasive. But the assessment has a further obligation: the current mood episode must be assessed and treated in its own right, and NICE CG78 states that when treating a comorbid condition in someone with borderline personality disorder, the guideline for the comorbid condition should be followed.[3] That single recommendation blocks the most common practical error, which is to attribute every new problem to the personality label and therefore to treat nothing. The same guideline also directs that young people with the diagnosis or with symptoms and behaviour suggesting it should have access to the full range of treatments and services within children and adolescent mental health services rather than being deferred until adulthood.[3]
depth.mistake: The first error is to convert a difficult encounter into a diagnosis. Difficulty is a property of an interaction, not of a person, and the encounter may be the first time anyone has listened. The second is the untreatable misconception, which the sources contradict: the RCPsych page explicitly labels it a misconception and devotes a section to improvement,[1] and NICE guidance for England includes specialist personality disorder services within trusts and a full range of recommended treatments.[3] The third is to let the label swallow the episode, so that depression, substance use, trauma responses and physical illness are read as expressions of the personality rather than as conditions with their own treatment. The fourth is the opposite omission: refusing to consider the pattern at all because the term feels stigmatising, which leaves a person with a long-standing, impairing difficulty and no formulation. The correction for all four is the same procedural discipline. Write three separated columns: the trait description in the person's and informants' words; the current state with its onset and course; and the context, meaning what is happening in the person's life and in the service relationship. Then state which threshold conditions are met, which are not evidenced, and what would need to be known. A pattern that fails one of the threshold conditions is still worth formulating; it is simply not the same claim.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. For this fictional case, write a one-page formulation with the three prescribed columns and then answer two questions in a sentence each. The case: a 24-year-old with a four-year history of intense relationships that end abruptly, two episodes of self-harm in the last year, and a current three-week episode of low mood and early waking after a relationship ended. Collateral history from a parent describes a similar pattern of intense friendships from age fourteen. Model response: column one holds the trait description with its developmental evidence, including the parent's account and the age of onset; column two holds the current episode, with its onset, duration, sleep change and severity; column three holds the context, including the recent ending and what the service has offered so far. The first question is which threshold conditions are met and which are not evidenced; the second is what would change the formulation. Self-review rubric, four points: are the three columns genuinely separate rather than decorative headings; is at least one threshold condition recorded as unevidenced; is the current episode given its own assessment and plan rather than being folded into the pattern; and does the formulation avoid evaluative adjectives about the person's character?
depth.summary: A personality disorder is a threshold claim about pervasiveness, duration and impairment, layered on top of an ordinary description of traits that everyone has. The claim has moved from ten categories to a severity and trait-dimension model, and the older names are now regarded as stigmatising even by the college that once used them. Two disciplines preserve accuracy: keep the trait description, the current episode and the context in separate columns, and treat your own reaction to the interaction as information to examine rather than as a finding to record. The next lesson turns to the assessment conditions under which the most sensitive material of all is gathered.

readings.title: Royal College of Psychiatrists, 'Personality disorder' (sections: 'What leads to a diagnosis of personality disorder', 'What different types of personality disorder are there?', 'Do people with a personality disorder diagnosis get better?')
readings.note: Read the opening paragraph on what the diagnosis is given for, then the severity ladder and the five trait domains, and note the statement that some of the pre-2019 category names are now considered stigmatising. The section 'Do people with a personality disorder diagnosis get better?' is written to counter the belief that improvement does not happen, and the section on help describes psychological therapies and the NICE position on short-term medication in crisis. Patient and carer information developed with people with the diagnosis, so treat it as an expert public-facing account rather than a clinical guideline.

readings.title: StatPearls, Personality Disorder (sections: Introduction, Epidemiology, Evaluation, Prognosis, Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes)
readings.note: Take the DSM-5-TR definition from the Introduction, including the clause about deviating from the norms and expectations of the surrounding culture. Read Epidemiology for the WHO-derived prevalence estimate and the three cluster estimates. Read Evaluation for the discussion of countertransference as something clinicians must recognise and can use as an evaluation tool. Read Prognosis for the antisocial personality disorder remission finding and Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes for its warning about preventing overmedicalisation or iatrogenic harm. Clinician-facing reference material, and hosts may sometimes present a verification step to automated requests.

readings.title: NICE CG78, Borderline personality disorder: recognition and management (recommendations 1.1.1.2, 1.3.6.3 and 1.5.1)
readings.note: Recommendation 1.1.1.2 states that young people with the diagnosis, or with symptoms and behaviour that suggest it, should have access to the full range of treatments and services within children and adolescent mental health services. Recommendation 1.3.6.3 states that when treating a comorbid condition in someone with borderline personality disorder, the guideline for that comorbid condition should be followed. Recommendation 1.5.1 concerns specialist personality disorder services within trusts. This guideline predates the dimensional reclassification described by RCPsych, so compare the two rather than reading either alone.

visual.title: Three columns feeding a threshold gate
visual.description: An instructional diagram separating trait description, current state and context, then passing them through a four-condition gate before any diagnostic threshold claim is made.
steps: Left column, headed Traits: record stable patterns in plain descriptive words, with the age of first evidence and who reported it.
Centre column, headed Current state: record what is happening now, with onset and duration, and label it as an episode rather than a trait.
Right column, headed Context: record current stressors, the service relationship, and any safety or access problems in the person's life.
Draw a gate with four labelled conditions: pervasive across contexts; inflexible; clinically significant distress or impairment; evident from adolescence or early adulthood.
Pass the three columns through the gate and mark each condition met, unevidenced, or not met - leaving unevidenced conditions visibly open rather than defaulting to met.

Below the gate, add two output boxes: 'threshold claim supported' and 'pattern formulated, threshold not evidenced', and note that both outputs still require the current episode to be assessed separately.

lessons.title: Trauma-informed assessment, and why a memory report is not a transcript
lessons.explanation: Trauma-informed assessment is a set of working conditions before it is a set of questions. It assumes that trauma is common rather than exceptional, that the person's control over what they disclose and when is part of the treatment rather than a courtesy, and that an assessment can itself cause harm if it is conducted in a way that re-enacts powerlessness. NICE's PTSD guideline gives concrete examples of what to avoid in the section on maintaining safe environments, warning against continued exposure to trauma-inducing environments and against triggers such as assessing or treating people in noisy or restricted environments, placing them in a noisy inpatient ward, or restraining them.[3] The second half of this lesson is epistemic. A person's account of a traumatic event is the best available information about their experience, and it is not a recording. Memory for an event is reconstructive, selective and changeable, and its formal qualities - vividness, gaps, emotion, consistency - do not by themselves establish or disconfirm what happened. That cuts in both directions and is why this lesson warns equally against treating a detailed account as proof and against treating an inconsistent one as fabrication. This is education about assessment reasoning with fictional examples; it is not a method for investigating or verifying anyone's history.
lessons.example: A fictional man describes an assault. He can give one fragment in sensory detail - the sound of a door and the colour of the light - and says the middle is 'blank', that the sequence afterwards is unclear, and that when he tries to describe it he feels he is 'making it up'. A colleague records 'narrative fragmented, query reliability'. Examine that. The relevant research does not support it. Rubin and colleagues tested coherence directly, asking people with and without PTSD to write narratives of their trauma and of comparison memories and to rate them for coherence, and concluded that memories of traumatic events were not more incoherent than the comparison memories, either in participants in general or in participants with PTSD, a result they describe as counter to most prevalent theoretical views of memory for trauma.[1] In a later review, Brewin describes how the debate has been refined: global narratives are usually well rehearsed, while disruptions and fragmentation are more likely to occur in episodic memories of the most frightening moments, and he notes that ICD-11 gives prominence to intrusive memories that have the quality of being relived in the present.[2] So both observations in the room can be true at once: a person can have a well-rehearsed summary story and one vivid, poorly contextualised fragment, and neither feature tells you what happened. The correct record is a description of the account, not a comment on its credibility. Something like: 'gives a detailed sensory fragment; reports a gap in the sequence; reports distress when describing it' records the same observations without making a finding the clinician is not in a position to make.
lessons.question: A fictional client's account of an assault is consistent in its overall shape but differs in detail each time she tells it, with more detail appearing after repeated questioning by different staff. What is the most defensible interpretation?
lessons.answer: That variability in detail with a stable gist is ordinary, and that repeated questioning by different people is itself a factor that can reshape an account
lessons.distractor: That the account is unreliable, because a genuine memory would not change across retellings
lessons.correction: Stability of gist with variation in detail is normal in autobiographical memory, and retelling is one of the conditions that shapes and elaborates a narrative. Changed detail is not evidence that nothing happened; neither is a detailed account proof that something happened.

depth.definitions: Trauma here means an event or series of events that is extremely threatening or horrific, including events from which escape is difficult or impossible. Trauma-informed practice adapts the conditions of care in light of how common trauma is; trauma-focused work is a treatment directed at traumatic memory, a different thing altogether. Re-traumatisation means the assessment or care setting itself reproduces elements of the original harm. Dissociation is a disruption in the normally integrated functions of consciousness, memory or identity; peritraumatic dissociation is dissociation occurring during or immediately after an event. An intrusion is an unwanted, vivid memory experience, and NICE's definition of complex PTSD describes it as arising after prolonged or repetitive events from which escape is difficult or impossible, with additional features of severe affect dysregulation, persistent beliefs of being diminished or defeated, and persistent difficulty sustaining relationships.[3] Narrative coherence is a property of a written or spoken account, not of a memory store. Episodic memory concerns a particular event; semantic memory concerns facts detached from a time and place.
depth.mechanism: Why is a memory report not a transcript? Four reasons do most of the work, and none of them implies the report is false. First, encoding under extreme arousal is selective. Attention narrows onto the features that seem immediately relevant, which is why a person may have an exceptionally clear fragment and almost nothing about the surrounding sequence. That is a difference in what was encoded, not in honesty. Second, retrieval is reconstructive. Recalling an event involves assembling it from retained fragments plus general knowledge, which is why repeated retelling gradually produces a more fluent, better-structured and often more detailed story. Third, the interview is a cause, not just a measurement. Leading or repeated questioning, institutional pressure to produce a version of events, and the identity of the listener can all shape what is produced, and the resulting confidence can be genuine without the content being accurate. Fourth, the formal features people use as an informal lie detector do not work reliably. Vividness, distress, physical signs of emotion, consistency and confidence are not validated markers of accuracy, and citing them as if they were converts clinical observation into an unlicensed verdict. None of this makes memory worthless. It makes it ordinary: good enough for gist and for personal meaning, unreliable for sequence and precise detail, and vulnerable to the conditions under which it is elicited. Brewin's review adds a further point about forgetting that is directly relevant to assessment. When considering how repeated events can be forgotten, he lists the way events have been framed by the perpetrator or other family members, whether the trauma has led to a fragmented sense of self, and whether there have been deliberate attempts to forget.[2] Those are features of the person's circumstances and coping, not evidence of veracity either way.
depth.secondExample: Take the mirror case and see how the same reasoning protects the person. A fictional client gives a detailed, chronologically ordered, emotionally flat account of an assault six years ago. Asked about the blanks other people report, she says she has told the story many times to police and at court, and has rehearsed it for that purpose. Here a well-organised narrative is the expected product of rehearsal, and a clinician who reads fluency as authenticity, or the absence of visible distress as indifference, has mistaken the conditions of the account for its content. Note also the trap of the opposite inference. A person who reports gaps or who describes the event in a flat, listless way may be reporting dissociative features, exhaustion, or cultural and interpersonal conditions that discourage display. In the same way, NICE's PTSD recommendations ask clinicians to be aware of traumatic events that may underlie presentations not framed as trauma at all, including for people with unexplained physical symptoms who repeatedly attend health services, and to consider asking about traumatic events with specific examples given.[3] The unifying skill is this: describe the account precisely, keep what you observed separate from what you inferred, and treat the presence or absence of formal memory features as information to be interpreted rather than as a verdict.
depth.mistake: There are two symmetric mistakes and a third that is procedural. The first is treating vividness, distress and detail as proof that an account is accurate, which turns the clinician into an investigator without the basis for the role. The second is treating gaps, inconsistency or flatness as proof that the account is unreliable or invented, which is the error the coherence research was designed to test, and which frequently reproduces exactly the disbelief that made disclosure costly in the first place. Both errors share a deeper fault: assuming that the purpose of taking a trauma history is to establish what happened. The clinical purposes are to understand the person's current difficulties, to avoid making them worse, and to decide what support is needed. A third, procedural error is arranging the assessment in ways that reproduce the original harm: retelling an account to a series of strangers, recording it in an environment the person cannot leave, or writing formulations in language that describes them as a container of symptoms rather than a person with a history. Correct the first two by deleting credibility judgements from the record and writing only what was said and observed, and by adding the clinical conclusion you actually need - distress, impairment, needs, safety. Correct the third by reviewing the physical and interpersonal conditions of the assessment before the content of the history, which is exactly what NICE's guidance on safe environments asks for.[3]
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. For this fictional case, write a four-part assessment plan in no more than one page, then answer two questions in a sentence each. The case: a 32-year-old is referred with unexplained chronic pain, repeated attendances at urgent care, and a history mentioned once, in passing, of an event at 19 that they will not describe. The four parts are: the physical and interpersonal conditions of the appointment; the questions you will ask and the words you will use; what you will not ask and why; and what you will record. The first question is how you will revisit the trauma history, if at all, and who controls that decision. The second is which of the clinical purposes - understanding difficulties, avoiding harm, deciding support - each part of your plan serves. Model response: conditions might include a room the person can leave, no interruptions, an agreed signal for stopping, and the option to write rather than speak; the questions would be about current sleep, pain, function and needs; what you will not ask is a precise sequence of events, because it serves no clinical purpose and risks harm; and the record would describe the account without credibility language and would state the distress and needs observed. Self-review rubric, four points: does the plan give the person explicit control of pace and stopping; are the questions about current functioning rather than about reconstructing an event; is there at least one thing you have decided not to ask, with a reason; and does the record contain no words that assess the account's truthfulness?
depth.summary: Trauma-informed assessment starts with the conditions of the encounter and ends with a record that describes rather than judges. Memory for traumatic events is ordinary memory under extraordinary conditions: selective at encoding, reconstructive at retrieval, and shaped by the interview that elicits it. Formal features such as vividness, gaps and consistency do not sort true from false accounts, and a clinician who treats them as though they did has exceeded their evidence in one direction or the other. The defensible practice is to describe precisely, infer cautiously, and keep the clinical purposes of the trauma history in view.

readings.title: Rubin, Boals and Berntsen, 'The Coherence of Memories for Trauma: Evidence from Posttraumatic Stress Disorder' (Consciousness and Cognition, PMC2928852), Abstract, the section on self-ratings of coherence, and the Discussion
readings.note: Read the Abstract first: participants with and without PTSD wrote narratives of their trauma and of comparison memories and rated them for coherence; based on self-ratings and naive-observer scorings, memories of trauma were not more incoherent than the comparison memories in general or in the PTSD group. The paper argues this is counter to most prevalent theoretical views. Read the 'self ratings of coherence' section for the pattern across studies, and the Discussion for the authors' own caveats about their undergraduate sample. Open-access author manuscript; the final edited version is in Consciousness and Cognition 2011;20(3):857-865.

readings.title: Brewin, 'Memory and Forgetting' (Current Psychiatry Reports, PMC6132786), Abstract and the sections on fragmentation and on why repeated events may be forgotten
readings.note: This review explains how the debate was refined rather than settled: global narratives tend to be well rehearsed, while disruption and fragmentation are more likely in episodic memories of the most frightening moments, and the author notes that ICD-11 highlights intrusive memories relived in the present. It also lists what must be considered when asking how repeated events could be forgotten, including how events were framed by a perpetrator or family members, a fragmented sense of self, and deliberate attempts to forget. Read it as a review of a live debate, not as a consensus statement.

readings.title: NICE NG116, Post-traumatic stress disorder (recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.5 and 1.4.1 to 1.4.5, with the 'Terms used in this guideline' entries for complex PTSD and acute stress disorder)
readings.note: Recommendations 1.1.1 to 1.1.5 cover recognition: the symptom domains to ask about specifically, the range of traumatic events, and the advice to consider asking about trauma in people with unexplained physical symptoms who repeatedly attend services. Recommendation 1.1.5 is a useful corrective to the assumption that trauma presents only as trauma. Then read 1.4.2 on maintaining safe environments, which warns against continued exposure to triggers such as noisy wards and restraint, and the definition of complex PTSD, which follows ICD-11 rather than DSM-5. Written for England.

visual.title: Account features that do not sort true from false
visual.description: A two-by-two instructional diagram crossing commonly used 'memory features' against their evidential value, showing why neither a detailed account nor a patchy one settles what happened.
steps: Draw a horizontal axis labelled Amount of detail, from very little to a great deal.
Draw a vertical axis labelled Expressed distress, from flat to extreme.

Place four labelled examples in the quadrants: a vivid fragment with a gap in the sequence; a fluent rehearsed narrative with no visible distress; a flat, sparse account; and a distressed, chaotic account.
Beside each example, write the legitimate observation - for instance 'well rehearsed for a court process' or 'reports blanks in the sequence' - rather than a credibility judgement.
Add a footer note: these features are not validated markers of accuracy, and none of them is a finding about whether an event occurred.

Add a side panel headed Clinical purposes listing the three uses of a trauma history - understand current difficulties, avoid causing further harm, decide what support is needed - and connect each to the assessment plan rather than to the question of what happened.

questions.prompt: A fictional trainee writes: 'client pulls out hair when anxious - diagnosis: hair-pulling disorder'. Which correction best reflects the symptom/strategy distinction?
questions.answer: The record describes an experience and an action with a stated function; the function and its evidence should be recorded before any category is considered
questions.distractor: The behaviour is self-directed and repetitive, which is sufficient for the category to apply
questions.correction: Repetition and form do not establish a category. The useful next step is to state the antecedent, the action and the consequence, and to mark the functional inference as an inference. The category question is a separate, criteria-governed step.

questions.prompt: Two fictional clients both stop attending a day programme. One describes dread in the group setting and relief on leaving; the other describes two months of early waking, appetite loss and inability to feel pleasure. What does the distinction between symptom and coping strategy add?
questions.answer: It generates different questions for each case: what the behaviour achieves for the first, and what has changed in the second person's functioning
questions.distractor: It shows that the first client is avoiding and the second is depressed, so the same behaviour has two diagnoses
questions.correction: The distinction is a reasoning tool, not a labelling shortcut. In the first case the reported relief is evidence about function; in the second, the observable withdrawal may be a consequence of reduced energy and reward rather than an attempt to manage distress.

questions.prompt: A fictional patient is described as anxious, tremulous and sleepless, with onset about ten hours after their last drink and gradual easing thereafter. A colleague records an anxiety disorder. Which correction is strongest?
questions.answer: The onset within hours of cessation and resolution with abstinence point to a withdrawal state, which should be reassessed after observed abstinence
questions.distractor: Anxiety and insomnia are specific to anxiety disorders, so the record is appropriate
questions.correction: Anxiety and insomnia are non-specific and appear in both explanations, so the timeline is the discriminating evidence. A withdrawal state also requires reassessment because severity can progress after initial presentation.

questions.prompt: A fictional young adult presents agitated and suspicious during several days of heavy stimulant use. A partner reports two weeks of unusual beliefs two months earlier, before the current use began. What should the formulation record?
questions.answer: Both a possible substance-related component and the possibility of a condition that persisted outside the use window, with an explicit reassessment plan after abstinence
questions.distractor: A substance-induced psychosis, because the current episode clearly began in the context of use
questions.correction: The earlier episode outside the period of use means the substance explanation cannot account for the whole history. Order of onset and course during abstinence are the discriminating observations, and neither is available from one interview.

questions.prompt: A fictional 27-year-old is referred for exhaustion and repeated sick leave. He says school was 'fine, I was just quiet', his mother organised everything until he moved out at 22, and he needs hours alone after work. What does the developmental frame require next?
