questions.answer: A cross-setting developmental history with the disappearance of earlier support recorded explicitly, alongside exclusion of current alternative explanations
questions.distractor: A diagnosis of an autism spectrum condition, because lifelong social difficulty and need for routine are present
questions.correction: A lifelong, cross-setting pattern raises the likelihood that a neurodevelopmental profile should be assessed, but current impairment, mood, sleep and other explanations must still be examined. The history changes which explanations are plausible; it does not complete the assessment.

units.title: Risk, treatment, recovery, and reading the evidence

lessons.title: Risk assessment and the real limits of prediction
lessons.explanation: Risk assessment in psychiatry is widely misunderstood as prediction, and the misunderstanding produces real harm in both directions. NICE's self-harm guideline is unusually blunt about this. Recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.4 state that risk assessment tools and scales should not be used to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, should not be used to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged, and that global risk stratification into low, medium or high risk should not be used for either purpose.[1] What the guideline directs instead is stated immediately afterwards: focus the assessment on the person's needs and on how to support their immediate and long-term psychological and physical safety, and undertake a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment.[1] The reason for that redirection is arithmetic as much as ethics. Serious outcomes are rare, and rare outcomes wreck the positive predictive value of any screening approach, so a tool that looks accurate in a validation paper can still label far more people wrongly than rightly when it is used to decide who gets care. This lesson teaches the formulation alternative and explains its limits. It is education about clinical reasoning with fictional and illustrative material; it is not a method for assessing anyone's risk, and no part of it should be used to judge whether a particular person is safe.
lessons.example: Take an illustrative population of 1,000 people and suppose that 1 per cent, ten people, will have the serious outcome in the following year. Now imagine a screening instrument that identifies 80 per cent of them and correctly clears 70 per cent of those who will not have the outcome. The arithmetic is unforgiving. Of the ten who will have the outcome, eight are flagged and two are missed. Of the 990 who will not, 297 are flagged because the specificity is 70 per cent. That gives 305 people flagged, of whom eight will have the outcome: about 2.6 per cent, meaning roughly 97 per cent of those flagged would not have had it. The same instrument, read as 'high risk', would have been used in good faith to restrict appointments, lengthen admissions, or discharge people as 'low risk'. This example is constructed for teaching and is not the performance of any real instrument. Its purpose is to show that prediction quality is a property of the instrument and the population together, and that the base rate does most of the work. It also shows why NICE's committee, explaining its own recommendations, recorded that risk assessment tools and scales cannot accurately predict risk, that using them to determine access to treatment or admission could lead to repeat self-harm, distress and lower patient satisfaction, and that the implicit message that risk is static outweighs any benefit the tools have as a communication aid.[2]
lessons.question: An illustrative instrument flags 305 people out of 1,000, of whom 8 go on to have the outcome and 297 do not. What does this show about using the result to decide who receives treatment?
lessons.answer: That most people flagged would not have had the outcome, so the tool cannot carry a decision about access to care on its own
lessons.distractor: That the instrument is faulty and should be replaced with a better one before any assessment is attempted
lessons.correction: The performance shown is the ordinary consequence of a low base rate. Replacing the instrument with a slightly better one changes the numbers but not the structure of the problem, which is why the guideline redirects assessment to needs and safety rather than to prediction.

depth.definitions: A risk factor is something statistically associated with an outcome. A risk marker is a measurable correlate; neither implies causation. Sensitivity is the proportion of those with the outcome who are correctly identified. Specificity is the proportion of those without the outcome who are correctly cleared. Positive predictive value is the proportion of those identified who actually have the outcome, and it depends heavily on the base rate, that is, how common the outcome is in the population being assessed. A static factor is fixed, such as a history of attempts; a dynamic factor can change, such as current intoxication, access to means, or the state of a relationship. Risk stratification sorts people into bands. A risk formulation is a collaborative, written account that describes the person's difficulties, needs, strengths and circumstances and states how safety will be supported. Safety planning is a joint plan of steps and contacts. Iatrogenic harm means harm caused by the care or its processes.
depth.mechanism: Three mechanisms explain why prediction fails, and each has a different remedy. First, base rates. When an outcome is rare, even a test with good sensitivity and specificity produces many more false positives than true positives, as the worked example shows. This is not a defect in a particular scale; it is a property of screening for uncommon events, and it is the reason a 'high risk' flag cannot mean what people assume it means. Second, the nature of the predictors. Risk-relevant features are common and non-specific: most people with a history of self-harm do not die by suicide, and many people with none of the listed features do. The WHO's suicide fact sheet addresses this directly, stating that the link between suicide and mental disorders - particularly depression and alcohol use disorders - and a previous suicide attempt is well established in high-income countries.[3] Two limits are buried in that sentence and both matter: the association is described as established in high-income countries rather than universally, and an established association is not a predictive test for an individual. Third, dynamics. Risk changes over hours; a formulation written on Tuesday may be wrong on Wednesday, and a stratified band creates precisely the illusion of stability that NICE's committee warned about.[2] The remedy the guideline proposes is to move the question from 'how likely is this person to come to harm' to 'what does this person need, what is their current situation, and how do we support their safety now and over time'. That reframing is not a rejection of careful assessment. NICE still requires a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment,[1] and it still asks services to consider needs, vulnerabilities and safety. What it rejects is the substitution of a band for a formulation, because a band discards the information a formulation preserves: what is changeable, what the person wants, who is involved, and what remains unknown.
depth.secondExample: Take a fictional inpatient whose checklist produced a 'low risk' score on admission. Over four days the person's relationship ended, their medication was changed, and they were told their leave was cancelled. On day five they harmed themselves. The tempting conclusion is that the assessment was performed badly. The better conclusion is that the method used asked the wrong question on the wrong day. A formulation would have recorded the changeable factors as they changed and would have flagged that the person's stated reason for wanting to leave was to see a partner, which the cancelled leave directly blocked. Now take the reverse case, equally fictional, in which a person with a long history of attempts and several static risk factors is described as 'high risk' and admitted under close observation for weeks. The static label changes nothing underneath: the aspects of the person's life that made those attempts more likely are untouched, and the observation ends when the bed is needed. In both cases, the missing element is the same: an account of what is happening in the person's life, what they say they need, and what would be done if things changed. A formulation can still be wrong, and it can still fail to anticipate an outcome; its advantage is that when it fails, it fails legibly, so it can be corrected.
depth.mistake: The first error is reading 'low risk' as 'safe'. The categories are not states of the world; they are outputs of an approach that the relevant guideline advises against. The second error is assuming a tool must be valid because it is widely used, or because it was validated somewhere. Validation is population-specific, and a scale developed in one service may not transport to another. The third is believing the goal is prediction at all, which leads to defensive documentation written to protect the service rather than to help the person. The fourth is the opposite over-correction: concluding that because prediction fails, nothing can be done, and therefore no safety consideration need be recorded. The guideline's own wording blocks that move, since it still requires a risk formulation alongside the focus on needs and safety.[1] A fifth error is forgetting the iatrogenic side. Restricting access, prolonging detention or discharging someone to manage an assessment band is an intervention with consequences, and the guideline's rationale names repeat self-harm, distress and lower satisfaction among them.[2] The correction for all five is procedural: never write a band without the formulation that produced it; never let a band determine access to care by itself; record which factors are changeable; and record what you do not know, because an acknowledged unknown can be monitored while a confident band cannot.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Rewrite a fictional stratified assessment as a formulation using seven fixed headings: needs; current stressors; changeable factors; who is involved and can be contacted; what the person themselves says would help; what remains uncertain; and what I would do if a named thing changed. The fictional assessment to rewrite reads: 'Risk: moderate. History of overdose. No current plan. Advised to contact services if thoughts worsen. Discharged.' Model response: needs might include a place to stay tonight, a treatment plan for a concurrent alcohol pattern, and an appointment within days; current stressors might include a relationship ending this week and a benefits decision pending; changeable factors might include access to means in the home; the person's own view might be that they need the appointment to be in the evening because of work; the uncertainty might be whether the alcohol pattern is escalating; and the conditional action might be what happens if they do not attend. Self-review rubric, four points: does the rewrite contain no risk band anywhere; is every entry a fact or an explicit uncertainty rather than an adjective about the person; are there at least two changeable factors; and does the conditional action name a specific observable change and a specific response?
depth.summary: Risk assessment is not risk prediction, and the difference is not a matter of opinion: the guideline prohibits prediction and stratification for these purposes and requires a formulation instead. Rare outcomes make positive predictive value collapse, predictors are common and non-specific, and risk changes faster than any band can. The formulation is not a softer version of assessment but a stronger one, because it keeps the information a band discards and fails legibly. The next lesson turns to the parallel question of how much confidence the treatment evidence itself can carry.

readings.title: NICE NG225, Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.6)
readings.note: Read section 1.6 'Risk assessment tools and scales' in full. Recommendations 1.6.1 and 1.6.2 prohibit using risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to decide who is offered treatment or discharged. Recommendations 1.6.3 and 1.6.4 extend the prohibition to global stratification into low, medium or high risk. Recommendation 1.6.5 redirects the assessment to the person's needs and immediate and long-term safety, and 1.6.6 requires a risk formulation as part of every psychosocial assessment. Note the definition of 'risk formulation' in the guideline's terms section. Written for England.

readings.title: NICE NG225, Rationale and impact, section on risk assessment tools and scales (recommendations 1.6.1 to 1.6.6)
readings.note: This is the committee's own explanation for the prohibitions, and it is the most useful page for understanding why they exist rather than simply that they do. It records that the committee agreed the tools cannot accurately predict risk, that determining access to treatment or admission from them could lead to repeat self-harm, distress and lower patient satisfaction, and that the potential harms of risk stratification - including the implication that risk is static rather than dynamic - outweighed its benefits as a communication tool. Read it alongside the recommendations, not instead of them.

readings.title: WHO, Suicide fact sheet (section 'Who is at risk?')
readings.note: Read the 'Who is at risk?' section for the statement this lesson uses: that the link between suicide and mental disorders, particularly depression and alcohol use disorders, and a previous suicide attempt is well established in high-income countries. Note the qualifier, which is the whole point - the association is population-level, not a predictive test, and the evidence base it describes is specific to high-income settings. The page also links the WHO mhGAP intervention guide module on suicide and self-harm. Public-health fact sheet, not clinical guidance, and its key-facts panel is rendered dynamically so read it in a browser.

visual.title: Why a good test still flags mostly the wrong people
visual.description: A counting diagram that follows 1,000 people through a screening decision, showing true positives, false positives, true negatives and false negatives, with the flagged box and the outcome box separated.

Within the band of 10, mark 8 as flagged and 2 as missed, and label the 8 'true positives'.
Within the band of 990, mark 297 as flagged and 693 as cleared, and label the 297 'false positives'.
Draw a single 'flagged' box holding 8 and 297, with a total of 305, and write beneath it: 8 in 305 is about 2.6 per cent.
Draw an arrow from the flagged box to a decision box labelled 'restrict access to care' and mark it with a warning symbol, because roughly 97 per cent of those inside would not have had the outcome.

Add a second panel replacing the band with a formulation template listing needs, changeable factors, who is involved, the person's own view, and uncertainties, and caption it 'keeps the information a band discards'.

lessons.title: What the evidence for psychological therapies does and does not support
lessons.explanation: Psychological therapies have a real evidence base, and the size of that evidence is smaller than the published literature suggests. Both statements have to be held at once, because collapsing either one produces a familiar error: either 'therapy is proven, so it will work for you', or 'the evidence is weak, so therapy is a placebo'. Reading the evidence properly means asking about the comparator, the outcome, the population, the dropouts and the completeness of the record, not just the direction of the result. A useful starting point is how a guideline defines the problem it is treating. NICE's depression guideline defines depression as a wide range of mental health problems characterised by absence of positive affect, low mood and associated emotional, cognitive, physical and behavioural symptoms, and states that severity exists along a continuum composed of three elements: symptoms, duration, and impact on personal and social functioning.[1] It then regards the categories as less severe and more severe, using a score of 16 on the PHQ-9 as the threshold in its own work.[1] That matters for interpreting trials, because 'depression' in a headline may mean anything along that continuum. This lesson is education about reading treatment evidence; it contains no treatment recommendations, no doses, and no advice about any individual.
lessons.example: Consider a headline that could plausibly appear anywhere: 'Talking therapy for depression works, large study finds'. A useful appraisal begins with the number that rarely reaches the headline. In a published systematic review and meta-analysis of US National Institutes of Health funded trials, the authors identified grants for randomised trials comparing psychological treatment with control or other treatments in adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder, checked whether each grant led to a publication, and obtained data from investigators where it had not. Thirteen of the 55 funded grants that began trials, 23.6 per cent, did not result in a publication. When the unpublished studies were added, the pooled estimate for comparisons with control conditions fell from a Hedges' g of 0.52 in the published studies to 0.39 overall, a reduction of about a quarter. The authors' conclusion is the sentence to carry: the efficacy of psychological interventions for depression has been overestimated in the published literature, just as it has for pharmacotherapy, and both are efficacious but not to the extent that the published literature would suggest.[2] Notice what that does and does not say. It does not say therapy does not work; the pooled estimate remained well above zero. It says the published number overstated the effect, and it explains one mechanism: studies with unhelpful findings are less likely to appear. The lesson is not that evidence should be distrusted generally, but that a specific and predictable kind of distortion has to be looked for, and that the tools for looking for it exist.
lessons.question: A fictional review finds that the pooled effect of a therapy fell from a Hedges' g of 0.52 to 0.39 once unpublished trials were included. What is the correct reading?
lessons.answer: The therapy retains a positive average effect, but the published literature overstated its size by about a quarter
lessons.distractor: The therapy is ineffective, because including the missing studies removed most of the apparent benefit
lessons.correction: The estimate remained above zero, so the effect was not removed, only reduced. The finding is about the size of the effect and about the distortion in the published record, not about whether the treatment works at all.

depth.definitions: Efficacy is performance under trial conditions; effectiveness is performance in ordinary services. A randomised controlled trial allocates participants to conditions by chance. The comparator may be a waiting list, treatment as usual, a placebo-like control, or another active treatment, and the choice changes what the result means. An effect size expresses the magnitude of a difference, in this literature usually Hedges' g, where about 0.2 is conventionally called small and 0.5 moderate. Publication bias is the tendency for studies to be submitted and accepted according to their findings. Outcome reporting bias is the selective reporting of some outcomes rather than others. Researcher allegiance is the association between an investigator's preferred treatment and the results they report. Response means a defined degree of improvement; remission means falling below a threshold. Common factors are elements shared by most therapies, such as the relationship, a rationale and the expectation of improvement; specific factors are the components unique to one approach.
depth.mechanism: Four mechanisms explain why the published evidence for psychological therapies overstates its case, and each has a corresponding question you can ask of any paper. The first is study publication bias: the Driessen analysis found that roughly one quarter of funded trials that began did not reach publication, and that including them reduced the pooled estimate by about a quarter.[2] The question to ask is whether the review searched beyond published articles, and whether protocols and registries were checked. The second is outcome reporting bias. In the same analysis the authors note a further limitation of their own work, that they could not examine outcome reporting bias quantitatively, meaning they could not check whether the outcomes reported were the ones originally planned.[2] The question is whether the primary outcome was pre-specified. The third is the comparator. A therapy compared with a waiting list answers a different question from the same therapy compared with an equally credible alternative, and the size of the resulting estimate depends on which was used. The question is what the participants in the control condition actually received. The fourth is the gap between average and individual. A pooled estimate describes the average participant in the included trials, who - as the paper's own data on who participates in trials implies - is often not the average person in a clinic. There is a genuine and unresolved debate about how much of the benefit of any therapy comes from factors common to all credible therapies rather than from the specific techniques of each school, and the honest position is that the question remains open rather than settled in either direction. A final mechanism concerns harms, which are reported far less systematically than benefits. Some people deteriorate during treatment, and reporting of deterioration is not standardised, which means the published record is better at telling you about average improvement than about who got worse.
depth.secondExample: Take two fictional studies with the same headline result and different epistemic weight. Study A was registered before recruitment, used concealed allocation, assessed outcomes by people who did not know which treatment the participant received, reported the pre-specified primary outcome with a confidence interval, used an intention-to-treat analysis, and published the full pre-specified secondary outcomes including the ones that did not favour the treatment. Study B was not registered, changed its primary outcome between the protocol and the paper, used an unblinded therapist-completed outcome measure, and reported only the scales that improved. Both may report a statistically significant benefit. They do not carry the same weight, and nothing in the headline distinguishes them. Now consider what a service needs. NHS information on talking therapies sets out what is available, how to access it, and the range of approaches, from guided self-help based on cognitive behavioural principles through to interpersonal therapy, couples therapy, EMDR and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, and notes that the type available depends on what is needed and on what is available locally.[3] That last clause is the effectiveness question in a sentence. What matters to a person is not the effect size of an approach in general but whether a suitable approach is available, accessible and tolerable to them, which is a different and more practical question than the one the meta-analysis answers.
depth.mistake: The first error is inferring individual benefit from an average effect. A pooled estimate describes a distribution, and the person in front of you is somewhere in it, sometimes below zero. The second is treating 'evidence-based' as a synonym for 'effective for me', when it means only that there is a body of evidence of a certain quality. The third is the cynic's error, concluding that because publication bias exists, all positive findings are worthless; that would discard the finding that the therapy retained a positive effect after the unpublished studies were added.[2] The fourth is ignoring attrition. In trials and in services, people who drop out are often those who were not helped, and an analysis of completers alone will flatter the treatment. The fifth is treating the common-factors debate as settled. It is not. The correction for all five is to replace the question 'does it work?' with five sharper ones: compared with what, measured how, in whom, with what proportion completing, and how complete is the record. Where the record is incomplete, say so; the Driessen authors do exactly that about their own analysis,[2] and that kind of self-limitation is a marker of a paper worth trusting.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. A fictional news article reports: 'New therapy halves depression in eight weeks'. Write five questions you would need answered before forming a view, and for each name the specific kind of bias or error it addresses. Model response: first, halves it compared with what - which addresses the comparator and whether a waiting list was used; second, was the trial registered and was the primary outcome pre-specified - which addresses outcome reporting bias; third, were the outcome assessors unaware of allocation - which addresses detection bias; fourth, how many assigned to each condition completed and how were those who did not handled - which addresses attrition and whether an intention-to-treat analysis was used; fifth, how many people were assigned, and how precise is the estimate - which addresses whether a large sample produced significance without a clinically meaningful difference. Self-review rubric, four points: is each question tied to a named bias or error rather than being a general expression of doubt; is at least one question about the people who dropped out; is at least one about the comparator rather than about the therapy; and does your answer distinguish a claim about average effect from a claim about any individual?
depth.summary: The evidence base for psychological therapies is real and its published magnitude is inflated, and the second fact does not cancel the first. Publication bias, outcome reporting bias, comparator choice, attrition, and the difference between average and individual effects are the levers, and each converts into a question you can ask of any paper or claim. The next lesson takes the same sceptical habit and applies it to the part of psychiatry that is least well served by a symptom-only frame: rehabilitation and recovery.

readings.title: NICE NG222, Depression in adults: treatment and management ('Definitions of depression and severity', and recommendation 1.1.1)
readings.note: Read the 'Definitions of depression and severity' block first: depression is characterised by absence of positive affect, low mood and associated symptoms; severity exists along a continuum composed of symptoms, duration and impact on functioning; and this guideline uses less severe and more severe rather than four categories, with a PHQ-9 score of 16 as the threshold in its own work. That tells you what 'depression' means when a trial or a service uses the word. Then read 1.1.1 on reducing stigma and barriers to help-seeking. Guidance for England; the severity sections are a useful reminder that effect sizes depend on who was recruited.

visual.title: Published estimate against the fuller record
visual.description: A two-tier figure showing a published pooled effect, then the same analysis with missing studies restored, with the change labelled rather than the conclusion.
steps: Draw a horizontal scale for effect size with a vertical line at zero labelled 'no difference'.
Plot the published pooled estimate as a marker with a confidence interval bar, labelled g = 0.52.
Below it, plot the fuller estimate after adding the unpublished studies, labelled g = 0.39, and draw a curved arrow between the two markers labelled 'about a quarter lower'.
List the missing studies as a small stack of boxes beside the lower marker, with a count of 13 of 55 grants that began trials and were not published.
Add a note beside both markers reading 'both estimates are above zero', to prevent the figure being read as a verdict of ineffectiveness.
