lessons.title: Rehabilitation and recovery-oriented practice
lessons.explanation: Two different things are called recovery. Clinical recovery means reduction of symptoms and of the need for services. Personal recovery means building a life that the person considers worth living, with or without continuing symptoms. The two are related but not interchangeable, and treating one as a proxy for the other has produced a great deal of avoidable harm. The most cited synthesis of personal recovery is the framework developed by Leamy and colleagues, which reviewed descriptions and models of personal recovery and arrived at five recovery processes that give the acronym CHIME: connectedness, hope and optimism about the future, identity, meaning in life, and empowerment.[2] NICE's guideline on rehabilitation for adults with complex psychosis provides the service-side counterpart, covering who should be offered rehabilitation, the principles, organising the pathway, improving access, a recovery-orientated approach, assessment and care planning, programmes and interventions, adjustments to mental health treatments, and physical healthcare.[1] Note the inclusion of physical healthcare in a psychiatric rehabilitation guideline; it is not an afterthought. This lesson is education about the logic of rehabilitation and recovery-oriented practice, not a treatment plan for any person.
lessons.example: A fictional person has been in contact with services for eleven years, has been admitted four times, and currently lives in supported accommodation. Two plans are written for the same person. Plan A says: continue current medication, attend the depot clinic, maintain symptom stability, review accommodation suitability in twelve months. Plan B asks the person what he wants, and he says he wants to work two mornings a week and to see his brother without a support worker present. Plan B then specifies what would be needed: a graded return to a structured activity with the option to stop, a vocational service that works with employers, a plan for what happens if he becomes unwell mid-week, and a review of whether his physical health needs are being monitored. Both plans are defensible in isolation, and only one of them would show up in a conventional outcome measure. Notice that Plan B does not remove treatment. NICE's guideline treats rehabilitation as a pathway that includes mental health treatment, adjustment of that treatment where needed, and physical healthcare,[1] and the WHO's report frames the necessary change as stronger community-based services rather than fewer services.[3] The distinction that matters is the target: symptoms in one case, a life and the supports that make it possible in the other.
lessons.question: A fictional discharge plan states: 'Symptoms stable for three months, therefore recovered. Discharge to independent living with no further support.' Which correction best reflects recovery-oriented practice?
lessons.answer: Stability is a clinical observation; a recovery-oriented plan would describe the life the person is building, the supports required, and what happens if stability changes
lessons.distractor: The plan is appropriate because three months of stability shows the person no longer needs services
lessons.correction: Reduced symptoms are not the same as a plan for living. Recovery-oriented practice keeps the supports that make the person's own goals possible and states how they would be restored if symptoms returned, rather than treating stability as the end of the work.

depth.definitions: Rehabilitation, in this context, is a structured pathway for people with severe and complex mental health problems who need help to develop or regain the skills, confidence and supports for community living. Complex psychosis is the population NICE's guideline addresses. Clinical recovery is symptom- and service-focused; personal recovery is defined by the person and concerns a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life, with or without continuing symptoms. Recovery-oriented practice organises care around the person's goals, strengths and community participation. Social inclusion means participation in ordinary settings such as work, education, housing and relationships. Supported employment means real employment with ongoing support. Peer support is help provided by people with lived experience. Functioning refers to what a person can do day to day, which is not the same as symptom severity. Coercion covers involuntary measures, and the WHO's report links reduction of coercion to human rights standards.[3]
depth.mechanism: Why is symptom change a poor proxy for what people want? Three structural reasons and one honest caveat. First, symptom scales measure the frequency and severity of experiences; they do not measure whether a person has work, friends, a place to live, or a reason to get up. The evidence base for rehabilitation is largely built on functional outcomes for precisely this reason. Second, the relationship between symptoms and function is loose. People with persisting symptoms function well when supports are adequate, and people with modest symptoms can be functionally stuck when they are not, which is why NICE's rehabilitation guideline treats the pathway, the environment and the person's goals as clinical variables rather than as context. Third, the processes identified in the CHIME synthesis are not symptoms at all: connectedness, hope, identity, meaning, and empowerment.[2] A framework built from people's own accounts of recovery will inevitably look different from a framework built from clinician-rated severity, and the fact that they diverge is information rather than a defect in either. Fourth, the caveat. Recovery language has been co-opted in some systems to mean that services can be withdrawn, which is the reverse of what the framework describes; a person who wants symptom-focused care is not failing at recovery. Related to this, the WHO's report situates mental health needs within services that are insufficient and inadequate worldwide so that no community-based support can be assumed, records that people with mental health conditions often experience stigma, discrimination and human rights violations, and frames its vision as participation free from stigma and discrimination.[3] It also works through the case for community-based services and against the persistence of large institutions. Read together with the guideline, this is a picture of what NICE calls a recovery-orientated approach operating inside a system that frequently cannot supply it.
depth.secondExample: Compare two ways of handling the same relapse. A fictional person has been in a supported tenancy for a year and has begun a part-time course. In the first approach, relapse triggers a review of suitability, and within a fortnight the tenancy is described as no longer appropriate; the person returns to a more supervised setting and the course ends. In the second, the plan written months earlier specified what would happen: who to contact, which medication review to request, what the course tutor would be told with the person's consent, and what level of support would be increased temporarily, with a stated point at which it would be stepped back down. The second approach is not more optimistic; it is more specific. It treats relapse as an anticipated event within a plan rather than as a verdict on the person's suitability, and it protects the thing the person said mattered. This is also how the CHIME processes operate in practice: connectedness through the maintained course and tutor relationship, hope through the stated expectation of return, identity through continuing to be a student, meaning through the purpose of the course, and empowerment through having set the conditions in advance.[2] The obligation this creates for services is concrete: the plan has to exist before the crisis, and it has to have been written with the person rather than about them.
depth.mistake: The first error is equating recovery with cure, so that any continuing symptom is recorded as a failure of the person's recovery. The second is equating recovery with discharge, which converts a framework about participation into a cost-saving instrument and withdraws exactly the supports the framework identifies. The third is imposing a recovery narrative: some people prefer to describe themselves as patients, want symptom-focused care, or reject the language of recovery entirely, and treating that preference as resistance is a misuse of the concept. The fourth is measuring the wrong thing. If a service's data capture symptom scores only, then the goals that matter to people will never appear in the record, and the service will keep optimising for what it measures. The fifth is treating rehabilitation as a low-status or palliative activity. NICE's guideline covers adjustments to mental health treatments and physical healthcare as core components,[1] which is a statement about clinical seriousness. Correct the first four by asking, at each review, two questions: what does this person say they are trying to build, and what support does that require, including the support needed if things change? Correct the fifth by noting that physical healthcare is part of the guideline and that people with severe mental illness have elevated physical health needs, which is a clinical task and not a lifestyle suggestion.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Rewrite this fictional discharge summary as a recovery-oriented plan of no more than one page, then answer two questions in a sentence each. The summary reads: '62-year-old male, 14-year history of psychosis, fourth admission. Symptoms now stable. Supported accommodation no longer required. Discharge to independent flat. GP to manage medication. No further follow-up required.' Model response: the rewrite should begin with what the person says he wants, which in the vignette he describes as cooking for himself again and attending the mosque on Fridays; it should name the supports those require, including transport on Fridays, a plan for the first four weeks at home, agreement on who he can contact and how, a physical health review covering the risks that NICE's guideline expects to be addressed, and a specified response if symptoms return. The first question is which of the CHIME processes each element serves; the second is what would be lost from this person's week if the plan were reduced to medication alone. Self-review rubric, four points: does the plan begin with the person's own stated goals rather than service goals; does it contain a pre-agreed response to relapse; does it include a physical health element; and does it avoid the words 'no further support required' in any form?
depth.summary: Clinical recovery and personal recovery answer different questions, and a service that only measures the first will keep losing sight of the second. The CHIME synthesis supplies the elements that come from people's own accounts, while NICE's rehabilitation guideline supplies the pathway, the treatment adjustments and the physical healthcare obligations. The main hazards are the co-options: recovery as cure, recovery as discharge, and recovery as a narrative imposed on people who prefer a different one. The next lesson examines how the language used about all of this can itself do harm.

readings.title: NICE NG181, Rehabilitation for adults with complex psychosis (Overview and the recommendation list, especially 'who should be offered rehabilitation', 'recovery-orientated rehabilitation services', 'rehabilitation programmes and interventions' and 'physical healthcare')
readings.note: Start with the Overview, which states the guideline aims to ensure people can have rehabilitation when they need it and promotes a positive approach to long-term recovery. Then follow the section links to who should be offered rehabilitation, the overarching principles, the recovery-orientated approach, person-centred care planning through assessment and formulation, and physical healthcare. Note that the Overview records the guideline was last reviewed in August 2024 and that the recommendations were developed before the coronavirus pandemic. Written for England.

readings.title: Leamy, Bird, Le Boutillier, Williams and Slade, 'Conceptual framework for personal recovery in mental health: systematic review and narrative synthesis' (British Journal of Psychiatry), Abstract and the section presenting the conceptual framework
readings.note: Read the Abstract: 97 papers were included from 5208 identified, and the resulting framework has three parts - 13 characteristics of the recovery journey, five recovery processes, and recovery stages. The five processes are connectedness, hope and optimism about the future, identity, meaning in life and empowerment, giving the acronym CHIME. The abstract also records that studies focused on recovery for people of Black and minority ethnic origin emphasised spirituality and stigma more, and identified culturally specific facilitating factors and collectivist notions of recovery. The article itself is paywalled; the DOI link resolves to the publisher landing page, where the abstract is free.

readings.title: Sandhu, Kilańska and colleagues, 'Personal recovery and its challenges in forensic mental health' (BJPsych Open, PMC8715254), Introduction paragraph on the CHIME framework
readings.note: This open-access review gives a short, accurate description of CHIME in its own words: a conceptual framework of personal recovery introduced by Leamy and colleagues, comprising the five recovery processes of connectedness, hope and optimism about the future, identity, meaning in life and empowerment. Read the Introduction only, as the rest concerns forensic services. Useful as a free companion when the original article is behind a paywall.

readings.title: WHO, World Mental Health Report: Transforming mental health for all (Overview page and publication landing page)
readings.note: Read the Overview statements that mental health needs are high worldwide and responses insufficient and inadequate, that the report calls for deepening the value given to mental health, reshaping environments, and strengthening systems, and its vision of a world where people can participate fully in society free from stigma and discrimination. The report was published in June 2022 and the full text is downloadable from the publication page at who.int/publications/i/item/9789240049338. It is a global policy report, not clinical guidance.

visual.title: Two targets, one plan: symptoms and a life
visual.description: A side-by-side diagram contrasting clinical recovery and personal recovery endpoints, with a single shared supports column that both depend on.
steps: Draw two vertical stacks. Left stack, headed Clinical recovery, lists symptom reduction, reduced admission, and medication review.
Right stack, headed Personal recovery, lists connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment as the five CHIME processes.
Beneath both stacks draw one wide bar labelled Supports: housing, money, work or study, relationships, physical healthcare, and crisis response.
Draw up-arrows from the supports bar into both stacks to show that a change in supports moves both outcomes, which is why withdrawal of support is not a neutral act.
Add a return arrow labelled Relapse plan looping from the supports bar back into the right stack, showing that relapse is an anticipated event inside the plan.
Add a caption noting that a discharge summary which records only the left stack has measured one of the two targets.

lessons.title: Stigma, language, and iatrogenic harm
lessons.explanation: Stigma is not an attitude that sits alongside clinical care; it changes care. The WHO's World Mental Health Report frames its vision as a world where everyone can participate fully in society free from stigma and discrimination, and the report treats stigma, discrimination and human rights violations as part of the problem it is addressing rather than as background noise.[2] Language is where much of that becomes concrete, because words do three things at once: they describe, they carry an attitude, and they shape what the next clinician will notice. The mental health charity Mind's guidance for talking about mental health, developed with people with lived experience, gives specific substitutions: describe someone as experiencing or living with a mental health problem rather than suffering from it; say died by suicide rather than committed suicide; avoid using clinical terms casually for everyday behaviour, such as calling an orderly person 'OCD' or a moody one 'bipolar'; and avoid slang that turns a diagnosis into an insult, including 'psycho', 'schizo' and 'split personality'.[1] NICE goes further and builds stigma into the required content of both information and training: recommendation 1.1.1 lists the impact of encountering stigma around self-harm among the topics to discuss with a person who has self-harmed, and 1.14.2 requires staff training to cover the stigma and discrimination associated with self-harm and the need to avoid judgemental attitudes.[3] This lesson is education about language and its effects, not a style guide to police anyone.
lessons.example: Two fictional discharge letters describe the same person and the same facts. The first reads: '34-year-old female, known borderline. Frequent attender, non-compliant with medication, presents with self-harm, attention-seeking. DNA'd two appointments. No psychiatric diagnosis made, no further follow-up required.' The second reads: '34-year-old woman with a long-standing pattern of intense relationships and episodes of self-harm, currently four months after a separation. Did not attend two appointments; she reports these were at times she could not arrange childcare, and this has been addressed by offering an evening slot. Attended today with distress and a mild injury. She describes urges to self-harm as a way of managing intrusive memories and says she does not want medication at present; her preference for psychological support has been recorded and discussed. A plan for the next four weeks is recorded.' Every clinical fact in the first letter survives in the second. What changes is what the second letter does. It records an explanation for the missed appointments rather than a character trait, it distinguishes the person's report from a judgement, and it makes the next appointment plausible. Notice also that the second letter does not conceal difficulty; it records distress, injury and a long-standing pattern. Precision and compassion are not in tension here; the vague letter is the less informative one as well as the more harmful one. The RCPsych page makes the same point in its own register, noting that the diagnosis can be upsetting and hurtful to receive but does not mean there is something wrong with who you are, and recording that some of the pre-2019 category names are now considered stigmatising.[4]
lessons.question: A fictional record states: 'Young woman, three overdoses this year. Manipulative. No mental illness, just personality issues.' Which correction best identifies the problem?
lessons.answer: It substitutes evaluative judgements for observed facts and drops the information a future clinician would need, which is both less accurate and more likely to affect care
lessons.distractor: It is too informal for a clinical record, but the clinical content is otherwise sound
lessons.correction: The difficulty is not the register but the substitution of judgement for information. 'Manipulative' and 'just personality issues' record nothing observable and discard the circumstances, the person's own account of the overdoses, and their needs. Rewriting it with the same facts is more informative, not merely politer.

depth.definitions: Stigma is a mark of discredit attached to a characteristic or group. Public stigma is held by others; self-stigma is the internalisation of those attitudes; structural or institutional stigma is embedded in rules, funding and practice. Discrimination is behaviour that disadvantages someone on the basis of such a characteristic. Diagnostic overshadowing is the attribution of new symptoms to an existing diagnosis so that other explanations are not considered. Iatrogenic harm is harm caused by care, or by its processes, rather than by the condition. Person-first language puts the person before the condition, as in 'a person living with schizophrenia'; identity-first language places the characteristic first, as in 'autistic person', and is preferred by many autistic people and by parts of the disability community. Sanism is prejudice against people with mental health conditions. Epistemic injustice describes the failure to treat someone as a credible source of knowledge about their own experience. Recovery-oriented language is language intended to support hope and agency, as used in the guidelines discussed in the previous lesson.
depth.mechanism: Why does language have clinical effects rather than merely social ones? Four pathways are worth separating. The first is help-seeking. Mind's guidance is explicit that stigma and the expectation of being dismissed make people less likely to seek support, which means the harm occurs before any clinician is involved. The second is the content of the record. A note is read by strangers, months later, without the person present; words that assert character rather than observation change what those readers consider plausible, which is diagnostic overshadowing in written form. The third is the interaction itself. If a person has previously been described as manipulative, they have good reason to manage what they say next, and the assessment yields less information. The fourth is structural: language shapes policy, and policy shapes who is admitted, funded and followed up. A further asymmetry deserves naming. Two genuinely competing preferences exist about labels, and both are legitimate. Some people find a diagnosis stigmatising; others need one to access services, benefits or accommodation, and the RCPsych page is honest about that tension when it explains why it still discusses the diagnosis.[4] Similarly, person-first language is widely recommended, and the Lancet Commission on ending stigma and discrimination in mental health recommends it while also concluding that decisions about which terms to use should be made by the people directly affected - a position this lesson treats as the practical rule. And some communities prefer identity-first language, or embrace language such as 'mad' as a reclaimed identity. The consequence for practice is to ask rather than assume, and to follow the person's preference for their own description while still holding the clinical precision standard.
depth.secondExample: The most damaging language is often the least dramatic. Consider three fictional entries, none of which contains an obvious insult. Entry one: 'Difficult historian, poor engagement.' Entry two: 'Reports that she stopped taking the medication after two weeks because of nausea and nobody told her what to expect; says she was not asked why she stopped.' Entry three: 'Brought by police after calling them herself.' Read for what each would do to the next clinician. Entry one closes inquiry and attributes the breakdown in information to the person's character. Entry two is longer and makes a plan possible: an adverse effect to address and an information gap to fill. Entry three records a fact that is easy to misread as evidence of escalation, when in this instance the person was seeking help and used the only route available at that hour. None of these three entries is false in the way the earlier letter was false; each is generatively wrong, in the sense that it produces a next step which is worse than the facts would justify. A useful test is to ask, of any sentence in a record, whether it would help a colleague who had never met the person to do something better. If it would only help them to form an impression, it does not belong there.
depth.mistake: The first error is reducing stigma work to word-policing, which invites the response that this is mere etiquette and therefore optional. NICE's guidance answers that directly by making stigma content part of what must be discussed with people who have self-harmed and part of what staff must be trained in.[3] The second is the assumption that using careful language is enough. A service can use exemplary phrasing while still offering nothing, and the same note can be warm and useless. The third is the belief that stigma is confined to the media or to the public, so that clinicians are exempt. The fourth is the opposite error, treating a diagnosis as inherently harmful and therefore withholding useful information about it, which overlooks the access and treatment functions described by the RCPsych.[4] The fifth is applying a single language rule across everyone. The correction for all five is to separate three questions that are often merged: is this statement accurate and observable; does this statement improve the next decision; and does this statement respect this person's own choice of how to be described? A record that satisfies all three is neither vague nor cold, and the earlier discharge letter example shows the second version is the more clinically complete one.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Rewrite the following fictional inpatient note so that every clinical fact is preserved and no evaluative judgement about the person remains. Note: 'Bed 9 - young man, drug-seeking, aggressive, no fixed abode, vague history. Threatens staff when asks for medication. Never satisfied. Would not engage with psychology.' Then answer two questions in a sentence each: which facts were missing that you could not invent, and which details you deliberately kept because they carry clinical weight. Model response: the rewrite might read that the person requested additional analgesia three times overnight, was verbally aggressive toward a nurse when a request was declined, reported sleeping in a hostel for the last two weeks, and declined a psychology appointment while saying he would attend a housing appointment; the missing facts would be his own account of the pain, his stated reason for declining psychology, and whether an alternative offer was made; the details kept because they carry weight are the aggression - which concerns the safety of staff and of the person - and the declined appointment, which matters for planning. Self-review rubric, four points: does every sentence describe something observable or something the person said; is there any word that describes character rather than behaviour; has anything clinical been removed in the name of being kind; and does the rewrite help a clinician who has never met him to act better?
depth.summary: Stigma operates through help-seeking, through the written record, through the interview, and through policy, and language is the mechanism by which all four are carried. NICE treats stigma content as part of required information and training, and Mind's guidance supplies concrete substitutions while insisting that the person's own preference governs how they are described. The discipline is not politeness but completeness: a record that substitutes judgement for observation is less accurate and less useful, and often more damaging, than the plainer one it replaced. The final lesson turns that scepticism onto the research literature itself.

readings.title: Mind, 'Talking about mental health' media guidelines (sections 'The power of language and stigma', the person-first guidance, and 'Discussing suicide')
readings.note: This PDF, developed with people with lived experience, supplies the specific substitutions used in this lesson: 'experiencing' or 'living with' rather than 'suffering from'; 'died by suicide' rather than 'committed suicide'; the warning that casually using 'OCD' or 'bipolar' for everyday behaviour trivialises real conditions; the instruction to avoid 'schizo', 'psycho', 'split personality', 'maniac', 'mad', 'nuts' and 'lunatic'; and the caution against 'attention seeking' for someone describing distress. It also states that preferences differ and that people with lived experience should be asked what language they prefer. A media-facing guide, so read it as an informed consensus document rather than clinical guidance. The link is a direct PDF download.

readings.title: NICE NG225, Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence (recommendations 1.1.1, 1.1.4 and 1.14.2)
readings.note: Recommendation 1.1.1 includes 'the impact of encountering stigma around self-harm' in the list of topics to discuss with a person who has self-harmed. Recommendation 1.1.4 asks services to recognise that information and support may need to be adapted for people who may be subject to discrimination, naming physically disabled people, people with neurodevelopmental conditions or a learning disability, people from underserved groups, people from Black, Asian and minority ethnic backgrounds, and LGBTQ+ people. Recommendation 1.14.2 requires training to include the stigma and discrimination usually associated with self-harm and the need to avoid judgemental attitudes. Guidance for England.

readings.title: WHO, World Mental Health Report: Transforming mental health for all (Overview, and Chapter 1 framing)
readings.note: Read the Overview for the report's vision statement - a world where mental health is valued, promoted and protected, where anyone can exercise their human rights and access care, and where everyone can participate fully in society free from stigma and discrimination - and for its framing that needs are high worldwide while responses are insufficient and inadequate. Read the report as a global policy analysis; it does not provide clinical definitions. The full text is downloadable from the publication page at who.int/publications/i/item/9789240049338.

readings.title: Royal College of Psychiatrists, 'Personality disorder' (section 'About this information' and the paragraph on upset at receiving the diagnosis)
readings.note: Two passages carry this lesson's argument: the statement that there are many reasons why personality disorder is a controversial diagnosis, and the passage beginning 'Being told you have a disordered personality can be upsetting and hurtful' followed by 'it does not mean there is something wrong with who you are'. The page also records that some pre-2019 category names are now considered stigmatising, and explains why the diagnosis is still discussed - because it can direct people to specific evidence-based support and allow access to services. That tension between stigma and access is the practical heart of the lesson.

visual.title: Same facts, two records, different next steps
visual.description: A two-column diagram showing the same clinical facts routed through judgemental wording and through descriptive wording, with the downstream decision attached to each.
steps: Left column: list facts only - separation four months ago, one injury, two missed appointments, childcare reported as the reason, request for psychological support.
Right column: place the judgemental version of the same facts - 'known borderline', 'frequent attender', 'non-compliant', 'attention-seeking', 'DNA'd'.
Draw two arrows from the fact list, one into each column, then draw a third arrow from each column into a decision box.
Under the judgemental column, the decision box reads 'no follow-up required'.
Under the descriptive column, the decision box reads 'offer an evening appointment and record the stated preference for psychological support'.
Add a footer line: 'every clinical fact survives the rewrite', and a side note naming the test - would this sentence help a colleague who has never met the person to act better?

lessons.title: How to read a psychiatric study critically
lessons.explanation: Appraising a study is a reproducible procedure, not a matter of taste. The tools are public and mostly free. The CONSORT statement is an evidence-based minimum set of recommendations for reporting randomised trials, now published as a 30-item checklist together with a flow diagram showing participants' progress through the trial, with SPIRIT providing a companion 34-item checklist for protocols.[1] The EQUATOR Network hosts a searchable library of reporting guidelines so that you can find the right standard for the design you are reading, whether that is a randomised trial, a systematic review or an observational study.[2] The Cochrane Handbook goes further and supplies the method for judging the evidence rather than merely describing it, with chapters specifically on considering bias and conflicts of interest among included studies, assessing risk of bias in a randomised trial, assessing risk of bias due to missing results, and completing summary-of-findings tables that grade the certainty of evidence.[3] National guidance bodies work to a published process as well: NICE sets out seven stages from topic selection through scope, evidence review, consultation, revision, sign-off and updating, and states that committees weigh the quality of the evidence, expert testimony, and how recommendations will be used in practice.[4] This lesson assembles those tools into a sequence you can run on any paper. It is education in critical appraisal, not a method for deciding what treatment anyone should receive.
lessons.example: Take a fictional paper reporting that a therapy reduced relapse. Run the sequence. Step one: who was in it? NICE's depression guideline, as a comparison point, treats severity as a continuum and uses a PHQ-9 threshold of 16 to separate less severe from more severe depression, so the first question is where this sample sits on that continuum and whether the recruitment route resembles your clinic. The appraisal literature is direct about this: patients who enrol in trials usually differ from the average patient, and the first table of a paper exists to let you check age, severity, duration and prior treatment.[5] Step two: what happened to them? Find the flow diagram and compare dropout between arms, because a treatment that people abandon for lack of benefit should show a higher dropout rate in the less effective arm; the same source calls this the 'voting with their feet' endpoint and notes it works from the patient's own perspective.[5] Step three: how was the comparison built? Look for concealed allocation and for blinding of whoever measured the outcome, since studies comparing blinded and unblinded assessment have found overestimation of treatment effects without blinding.[5] Step four: is the analysis intention-to-treat? That means everyone randomised is analysed in their assigned arm, and per-protocol analysis, when presented, belongs after the intention-to-treat results and not instead of them.[5] Step five: how big and how precise? A very large study can produce statistical significance from a difference too small to matter, while a small study can miss a real effect; the remedy is to read the effect size and its confidence interval rather than the p-value alone, and to convert to an absolute measure such as the number needed to treat.[5] Step six: what does the generalisation claim require? Here the causal-inference literature adds a point that is easy to miss: randomisation removes confounding from variables whether or not they were measured, but a trial's participants are a convenience sample accrued as they arrive, so moving from 'the treatments differed in this sample' to 'this treatment applies to my patient population' needs a further transportability assumption that is usually unstated.[6] Step seven: what does the wider record show? The same source documents the 'winner's curse': because negative phase-three trials are less likely to be published, published effect estimates are biased upward and tend to shrink on replication.[6] Nothing in these seven steps requires statistics beyond the paper's own tables.
lessons.question: A fictional trial reports a statistically significant benefit, a dropout rate three times higher in the control arm, and a primary outcome that differs from the one in its registration record. What is the most defensible appraisal?
lessons.answer: The differential dropout supports a real perceived benefit, but the changed primary outcome means the significance of the reported outcome cannot be taken at face value without the pre-specified analysis
lessons.distractor: The trial is sound, because randomisation and a significant result are the two requirements for a treatment to be considered effective
lessons.correction: Randomisation and a p-value are not sufficient. A primary outcome that changed after registration is the definition of a reporting problem, and the pre-specified outcome must be examined. The differential dropout is genuine positive evidence and sits alongside the reporting problem rather than cancelling it.

depth.definitions: Internal validity is whether the comparison within a study is sound; external validity is whether the result applies outside it. Confounding is a distortion produced by a variable that influences both the exposure and the outcome. Randomisation allocates participants by chance and removes confounding by any factor, measured or not. Random sampling selects participants from a population by chance, and a trial almost never does this. Allocation concealment hides the next assignment from whoever enrols participants. Blinding prevents participants or assessors from knowing the allocation. Intention-to-treat analysis includes all randomised participants in their assigned arm; per-protocol analysis includes only those who received the intervention as specified. Attrition is loss of participants after randomisation. An effect size quantifies the magnitude of a difference; a confidence interval expresses its precision. The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. A surrogate outcome substitutes a laboratory or intermediate measure for a clinical one. Pre-registration is the public recording of design and outcomes before recruitment. The winner's curse is the upward bias in published effect estimates produced by selective publication of positive results. A reporting guideline is a checklist for describing a study, not a certificate of its quality.
depth.mechanism: The sequence works because each step removes a different class of error. Randomisation addresses confounding. Concealed allocation addresses selection of who enters which arm. Blinding addresses measurement bias, which is why unblinded assessment inflates effects. Intention-to-treat addresses attrition, because people who leave a trial are systematically different from those who stay, and analysing only completers flatters the treatment. Effect sizes with confidence intervals address the confusion between statistical significance and clinical importance, which arises because significance depends on both the size of the difference and the precision of the estimate. Pre-registration addresses outcome switching. Searching beyond published articles addresses publication bias. Two limits of the sequence deserve stating. The first is that reporting tools are about reporting. The CONSORT statement says so itself, describing a minimum set of recommendations for reporting rather than for design or conduct, and noting the incidental hope that transparent reporting reveals deficiencies that would otherwise stay hidden.[1] A paper can complete every checklist item and still describe a study that should not change practice; conversely, a badly reported but well-conducted trial is a real occurrence, which is why the appropriate response to incomplete reporting is to ask the authors rather than to conclude the study failed. The second limit is generalisability. Random allocation supports a comparison between treatments inside a sample; it says nothing about whether your patient resembles that sample. The appraisal literature puts this plainly: because participants are accrued over time subject to entry criteria, the sample is a convenience sample, and interpreting a group-level statistic as an estimate for a patient population requires an additional assumption of transportability.[6] So the final question is never 'was the study significant' but 'how big, how precise, in whom, compared with what, and how much of the record am I able to see'.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same sequence to a fictional observational study reporting that a factor 'doubles the risk' of a later diagnosis. The first difference is design: there was no randomisation, so confounding is not removed and must be addressed by design and by analysis. The second is that a doubled relative risk can be trivial or important, depending entirely on the absolute risk. If the baseline rate is 1 in 1,000 and it rises to 2 in 1,000, the relative risk is 2.0 and the absolute increase is one extra case per 1,000 people; the number needed to harm is 1,000. The third is reverse causality: an early feature of the condition may itself change the exposure, so the direction of the association cannot be assumed from timing alone. The fourth is detection bias, which is acute in psychiatry: if the factor in question brings someone into contact with services more often, then more diagnoses will be recorded in that group whether or not the underlying condition is more common. The observational report and the randomised report therefore require different questions at every step, which is why the EQUATOR library is organised by study design rather than offering a single checklist.[2] Note also what the two designs share: in both, the honest summary states the magnitude, the precision, the population, and the residual uncertainty, and neither supports an individual prediction about a named person.
depth.mistake: The first error is reading the abstract and stopping. Abstracts omit the comparator details, the attrition figures and the confidence intervals that decide the paper's weight. The second is treating p below a threshold as the answer to whether a treatment matters, when it answers a narrower question about the probability of the data under a null hypothesis, and is sensitive to sample size. The third is assuming peer review guarantees correctness; journals review reporting and plausibility, not the truth of the underlying data, and the Driessen analysis discussed earlier in this level found a quarter of funded trials simply unpublished.[7] The fourth is treating a completed checklist as evidence of quality; CONSORT explicitly concerns reporting, not design, conduct or analysis.[1] The fifth is reading an observational association as causal, or a randomised result as generally applicable, which are opposite errors produced by the same failure to ask what the design licenses. The sixth is ignoring harms and dropouts, which are the information most relevant to a person deciding whether to continue. Correct the first by reading the methods and the first table before the conclusion. Correct the second by converting to absolute effects. Correct the fifth by writing, in one sentence, what the design licenses and what it does not; if you cannot write that sentence, you have not yet finished appraising the paper, whatever else you have read.
depth.application: Task, non-blocking. Take any published randomised trial in mental health - choose one from a source named in the readings if you like - and answer eight questions on one page: who was recruited and how; what the comparator received; whether allocation was concealed and who was blinded; how many were randomised and how many completed in each arm; whether the analysis was intention-to-treat; what the primary outcome was and whether it was pre-specified; the effect size with its confidence interval, converted to an absolute measure if the outcome is binary; and what the design does and does not license. Finish with a single sentence stating what you would need to know before this changed anything about care. Model response for the closing sentence: something of the form 'this shows that treatment A performed better than treatment B in a sample recruited through X, and does not show that it would do so for the people who attend our service, whose treatment history and severity differ in these specific ways'. Self-review rubric, four points: did you read the methods before the conclusion; is the comparator identified by what participants actually received; is the effect expressed both relatively and absolutely; and does your final sentence avoid the word 'proven'?
depth.summary: Critical appraisal is a short, repeatable sequence: who was studied, what happened to them, how the comparison was built, how the analysis handled attrition, how big and precise the effect was, what the design can and cannot license, and how complete the wider record is. The tools are public, and the two most useful habits are knowing which question each design can answer and knowing that significance is not importance. That is the end of this level, and the habit it leaves is the one that ought to have been present throughout: describe what you observed, name the strength of what supports it, and state what remains uncertain.

readings.title: SPIRIT-CONSORT, the CONSORT 2025 statement and checklist, and the SPIRIT 2025 protocol checklist
readings.note: The site now operates as the joint SPIRIT-CONSORT website; the older consort-statement.org address redirects here. Read the description of CONSORT as an evidence-based minimum set of recommendations for reporting the results of randomised trials, comprising a 30-item checklist and a participant flow diagram, and of SPIRIT as a 34-item checklist for protocols. Note the site's own warning that the checklist should be used with the Explanation and Elaboration document. This is a reporting standard, not a quality score: it tells you whether a trial was described completely, not whether it was well conducted.

readings.title: Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (current version), Chapter 8 'Assessing risk of bias in a randomized trial', Chapter 13 'Assessing risk of bias due to missing results in a synthesis', Chapter 14 'Completing Summary of findings tables and grading the certainty of the evidence', and Chapter 15 'Interpreting results and drawing conclusions'
readings.note: Read the chapter titles on the contents page first to see the structure, then open Chapter 8 for the domains used to judge risk of bias in a trial, and Chapter 13 for the specific problem of missing results - the formal version of the publication-bias problem discussed in lesson 47. Chapter 14 introduces the approach to grading certainty of evidence, and Chapter 15 covers interpretation. The Handbook is the methodological reference for systematic reviews and is written at a technical level; read the introductory paragraphs of each chapter before attempting the detail.

readings.title: Chu, 'How to read a clinical trial paper: a lesson in basic trial statistics' (PMC3380258), sections on the study sample, dropout, study design bias, intention-to-treat analysis, and effect size
readings.note: This is the closest thing to a worked checklist for the sequence in this lesson. Read the section on whether the subjects resemble your patients, and note the mock irritable bowel syndrome example showing that samples recruited from primary care, from specialists and from newspaper advertisements differed significantly. Read the dropout section for the 'voting with their feet' endpoint, the design section for allocation concealment and blinding, the intention-to-treat section, and the sections on p-values, confidence intervals and number needed to treat. Open access review written for clinicians.

readings.title: EQUATOR Network Library
readings.note: The Library is described on its own front page as a comprehensive searchable database of reporting guidelines, and it also links to related resources for writing and publishing health research. Use the search to find the appropriate guideline for whatever design you are reading - for example a trial, a systematic review or an observational study - rather than assuming one checklist applies to all of them. A resource directory, not a source of evidence in itself.

readings.title: NICE, 'How we develop NICE guidelines' (Process steps 1 to 7, and 'How we use evidence to inform recommendations')
readings.note: Read the seven process steps in order - topics chosen, scope produced, guideline developed, draft consulted on, comments considered, sign-off, updating - and note the point at which a committee of practitioners, people who use services and carers sees the quality-appraised evidence. Then read 'How we use evidence to inform recommendations', which states that committees consider the quality of the evidence, expert testimony, and how the recommendations will be used in practice. This shows you what a guideline is: a judgement by a named committee against a published process, which means it can be read critically and argued with, not merely obeyed. NICE guidance applies to England.

readings.title: van Zwet and colleagues or equivalent, 'Interpreting Randomized Controlled Trials' (PMC10571666), Abstract and the discussion of randomisation versus random sampling and of the winner's curse
readings.note: Read the Abstract for the two ideas used in this lesson: that random treatment assignment removes bias and confounding from variables other than treatment, while obtaining a representative random sample is effectively impossible because trial participants are accrued sequentially and so form a convenience sample; and that the 'winner's curse', produced by the lower likelihood of publishing negative phase-three trials, biases published effect estimates upward and leads them to shrink on replication. Technical in places, so read the plain-language summary and the abstract before the body.

visual.title: Seven-step appraisal cascade
visual.description: A cascade diagram routing one paper through seven sequential questions, with a stop point at each step where the answer would change how much confidence the paper can carry.
steps: Step 1, Who: was the sample like the people this question is about, judging by the first table - age, severity, duration, prior treatment.
Step 2, What happened: compare dropout between arms on the flow diagram, and note that leaving for lack of benefit is itself an outcome.
Step 3, How compared: was allocation concealed, and who was blinded - participant, clinician, or the person measuring the outcome.
Step 4, How analysed: were all randomised participants analysed in their assigned arm, and if a per-protocol result is shown, is the intention-to-treat result shown first.
Step 5, How big and how precise: plot the effect size with its confidence interval, and convert to an absolute measure such as the number needed to treat.
Step 6, What it licenses: state in one sentence what the comparison supports inside the sample, and what the move to a wider population would additionally require.
Step 7, What the record shows: check registration against the reported primary outcome, and consider what unpublished trials in the same area would be likely to show.

questions.prompt: A fictional inpatient checklist records 'moderate risk' for a person who then, four days later after a relationship ended and leave was cancelled, harmed themselves. A colleague concludes that the initial assessment was performed badly. Which correction is strongest?
questions.answer: The method asked a predictive question that cannot be answered reliably and treated a changing situation as static, so the failure was structural rather than a lapse in effort
questions.distractor: The assessment was performed badly because a serious outcome followed a moderate rating
questions.correction: The guideline prohibits using tools and stratification to predict these outcomes and directs assessment to needs and safety with a risk formulation. A band cannot track change, so a deteriorating situation can produce a correct-sounding score on the wrong question.

questions.prompt: A fictional service proposes to use a validated scale to decide who is admitted after self-harm. Using the guideline and the base-rate logic, which response is best?
questions.answer: Decline the use of the scale for that decision, keep a needs-and-safety formulation, and record how safety will be supported over time
questions.distractor: Accept it, provided the scale has been validated in a population similar to the local one
questions.correction: Validation in a similar population improves performance but does not remove the prohibition or the base-rate problem: most people flagged would not have the outcome, so the scale cannot carry a decision about who receives care.

questions.prompt: A fictional service reports that mean symptom scores improved by a third and concludes that recovery-oriented practice is now in place. Which correction is best?
questions.answer: Symptom change measures clinical recovery; a recovery-oriented account would also describe the person's own goals and the supports and connections that make them possible
questions.distractor: A third improvement in symptoms is a reasonable proxy for personal recovery in the absence of other data
questions.correction: The two targets are different, and the CHIME processes - connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment - are not symptoms. A service measuring only severity will keep optimising for what it measures and will not record what the person is trying to build.

questions.prompt: A fictional discharge summary says a person who wanted to return to part-time work is 'recovered' after three stable months, and closes the case. Which correction best reflects the recovery literature and the rehabilitation guideline?
questions.answer: Stability is a clinical observation, not an endpoint; the plan should state the supports the person's goal requires and the agreed response if stability changes
questions.distractor: The conclusion is sound because three months without symptoms meets the definition of recovery
questions.correction: Recovery in the personal sense is defined by the person and can include continuing symptoms, while the rehabilitation guideline treats treatment adjustments, physical healthcare and the pathway as continuing clinical work. Closing the case converts recovery language into withdrawal of support.

questions.prompt: A fictional record describes a woman as 'manipulative, non-compliant, attention-seeking' after three self-harm presentations. Which correction identifies both the accuracy and the care problem?
questions.answer: Judgements have replaced observations, so the record is both less informative for the next clinician and likely to change how she is treated
questions.distractor: The phrasing is unprofessional, but the clinical meaning of the terms is clear to other clinicians
questions.correction: The problem is not register but substitution: nothing observable is recorded, the circumstances and the person's own account are lost, and the words that remain shape the next decision. NICE treats stigma content as required information and training, not as etiquette.

questions.prompt: A fictional man of 51 is brought to an emergency department on day four after stopping heavy drinking, with fever, sweating, disorientation, agitation and visual hallucinations. A colleague records 'first episode of psychosis, commence antipsychotic'. Using the symptom-strategy distinction, the withdrawal evidence and the timeline discipline, write the correction you would make. Which longest-form answer is strongest?
questions.answer: This is a withdrawal-state emergency requiring urgent medical assessment: the disorientation, fever and autonomic signs with day-four timing match the described severe end of alcohol withdrawal, and the 'psychosis' reading both misnames the problem and discards the information that makes it urgent
questions.distractor: The hallucinosis supports a psychotic episode and the drinking was a coping strategy, so the priority is a formulation covering both the psychosis and the drinking
questions.correction: Hallucinosis and disorientation are the described features of withdrawal rather than a first psychotic episode, and the severity and timing are the clinically decisive facts. Treating it as functional psychosis also delays the assessment it needs. Withdrawal severity can progress, so reassessment over time is part of the correction, not an afterthought.

questions.prompt: A fictional woman of 29 is described as having 'suspected emotionally unstable personality disorder' after three months of intense relationships, one episode of self-harm, and a recent separation. She has no history of such difficulties before this year. Which answer best applies the threshold logic and the language discipline together?
questions.answer: The threshold is not evidenced, because pervasiveness and a course from adolescence or early adulthood are required and a three-month onset weighs against them, and the label should not appear in the record while the current episode and context are being assessed
questions.distractor: The pattern is clear enough for a provisional diagnosis, and recording it will help her access the appropriate psychological therapy
questions.correction: A required condition of the claim - a course beginning in adolescence or early adulthood - is currently unevidenced, so the label is premature whatever its access benefit. The three separated columns are the alternative: traits described in her own words, the current episode with its own assessment, and the context.

questions.prompt: A fictional 41-year-old refers himself for 'burnout'. His account: two years of needing to recover in a dark room after any social event, lifelong difficulty telling whether a remark was hostile, one intense interest since childhood, and repeated sick leave since a restructuring. He says school was fine because his mother managed everything. He denies low mood. Which answer best integrates the developmental and the alternative-explanation reasoning?
questions.answer: A cross-setting developmental history should be taken with the disappearance of earlier scaffolding dated explicitly, while mood, sleep, physical and substance explanations and current impairment are still assessed, because a lifelong pattern raises the likelihood of a neurodevelopmental profile without establishing it
questions.distractor: The lifelong pattern across settings and his lack of low mood make a neurodevelopmental profile the explanation, so the assessment can move to support planning
questions.correction: The history changes which explanations are plausible and adds the detail that matters most - that support fell away while demand rose - but current impairment, alternative causes and the impact on daily functioning still require assessment. The absence of low mood removes one alternative rather than completing the picture.

questions.prompt: A fictional 68-year-old is described by his daughter as 'inflexible and unable to cope' since his wife died. He reports the same rigid daily order for forty years, two close friends, and distress whenever plans change, which she confirms was always true. A week's screening instrument rates him 'low risk, no follow-up'. Two errors are in play. Which answer identifies both?
questions.answer: A lifelong, non-deteriorating pattern has been read as a new decline, and a stratified band has been used in place of a formulation that would have recorded what changed - the loss of scaffolding - and what support is now needed
questions.distractor: A mood disorder has been missed because the screening instrument covered only risk, and the lifelong pattern shows that this is a personality difficulty rather than a disorder
questions.correction: The history is of no change from baseline, so the difficulty is a long-standing profile meeting a changed environment, not a decline. Separately, the guideline prohibits using stratification to determine follow-up and requires a needs-and-safety formulation, which is what would have captured the changed circumstances.

questions.prompt: A fictional client describes a violent assault. She gives one detailed sensory fragment, reports a gap in the sequence, and says she fears she is inventing it. Different staff ask her to retell it on four occasions; the account becomes more detailed each time. A colleague writes 'detail increasing under questioning, query fabrication'. Which response is most defensible?
questions.answer: Record what she reported and observed without credibility judgements, and change the assessment conditions: repeated questioning is itself a condition that reshapes an account, and increases in detail under those conditions are not evidence of fabrication
questions.distractor: Record the escalation of detail as a concern about reliability, since a stable account would be expected if the event had occurred
questions.correction: The coherence research found trauma memories no less coherent than comparison memories, and retelling is a recognised influence on narrative form, so neither gaps, nor vivid fragments, nor elaborated detail sort true from false accounts. NICE separately asks for assessment conditions that do not re-expose people to trauma-related triggers.

questions.prompt: A fictional service wants to 'risk stratify' all new referrals, arguing that stratification allows scarce psychological therapy places to go to the most urgent cases and that no alternative exists. Using the guideline, the rationale document and the base-rate arithmetic, which answer is strongest?
questions.answer: The guideline prohibits stratification for deciding who is offered treatment, the rationale records that this could lead to repeat self-harm and distress, and the arithmetic shows most flagged people would not have the outcome, so the scarce-place argument fails on its own terms
questions.distractor: Stratification is acceptable for allocating scarce resources as long as assessment of needs and safety also takes place, because rationing decisions have to be made somehow
questions.correction: Recommendation 1.6.2 prohibits using tools and scales to decide who should and should not be offered treatment, and 1.6.4 prohibits stratification for the same purpose. The low positive predictive value means the flag does not identify urgency, so it cannot perform the rationing function claimed for it. The needs-based assessment it displaces is the defensible alternative.

questions.prompt: A fictional headline reads: 'Therapy halves relapse, major trial shows.' The linked paper is registered, but its reported primary outcome differs from the registered one, dropouts are 9 per cent in the treatment arm and 27 per cent in the control arm, and the confidence interval around the effect is wide. Which appraisal is most defensible?
questions.answer: The differential dropout is genuine evidence of perceived benefit and should be reported, while the changed primary outcome and the wide interval mean the headline figure cannot be relied on until the pre-specified outcome is examined
questions.distractor: The trial is unreliable in every respect, since an outcome change after registration invalidates the whole result and nothing should be taken from it
questions.correction: Each finding carries its own weight. Dropout asymmetry is the 'voting with their feet' evidence that participants themselves experienced a difference. Outcome switching is a distinct reporting problem that requires the pre-specified result, and the wide interval means precision is limited. Neither cancels the other.

questions.prompt: A fictional review of therapy for depression pools published trials and reports a moderate effect. A trainee proposes checking no further, because the studies were peer reviewed. Using the evidence on publication bias and the appraisal sequence, which answer is strongest?
questions.answer: Peer review does not address whether unpromising trials were published or whether outcomes were switched, and in this literature a substantial proportion of funded trials went unpublished and the pooled estimate fell by about a quarter when they were restored
questions.distractor: Peer review is sufficient for published trials, so remaining uncertainty concerns only how the effect generalises to local services
questions.correction: The Driessen analysis found 13 of 55 funded grants that began trials did not result in publication and that restoring them reduced the pooled estimate by about a quarter, which is precisely the distortion peer review cannot detect. Generalisability is a separate question, not the only one remaining.

questions.prompt: A fictional person in rehabilitation says he wants two mornings of work a week, not fewer symptoms. His care coordinator objects that work will destabilise him and proposes to wait for a further six months of stability. Which answer best applies rehabilitation and recovery reasoning?
questions.answer: The aim should be to build the graded activity and supports the person's goal requires, with an agreed response if things change, since the rehabilitation pathway includes treatment adjustment, physical healthcare and a recovery-orientated approach rather than symptom stability as a precondition
questions.distractor: Stability should come first, because employment is a stressor and the recovery framework prioritises clinical improvement before participation
questions.correction: Clinical and personal recovery answer different questions, and the CHIME processes concern connectedness, hope, identity, meaning and empowerment rather than symptom thresholds. The pathway NICE describes treats the person's goals, the supports they need and the response to relapse as clinical work, which is compatible with treatment continuing rather than replacing it.

questions.prompt: A fictional ward round records a person as 'no insight, difficult, frequently requests PRN'. A week later she is discharged, and the summary repeats 'no insight'. Nothing records why she was requesting medication or what she said about it. Which answer names the accuracy and care failures and the practical remedy?
questions.answer: The record substitutes judgement for observation and drops her account and circumstances, which is less informative for the next clinician and likely to affect her care; the remedy is a rewritten entry giving observable facts and her own report, with any clinical content you cannot verify labelled unknown
questions.distractor: The entry is incomplete but not harmful, because 'no insight' is a recognised clinical descriptor recorded routinely in psychiatric practice
questions.correction: 'No insight' asserts a conclusion the record does not support and, repeated in a summary, follows the person after discharge. Stigma and judgemental content are treated by NICE as matters for required information and staff training, and the practical test is whether the sentence would help a colleague who has never met her to act better.

questions.prompt: A fictional 22-year-old presents with agitation, unusual beliefs about neighbours, and heavy cannabis use for two months, after a job loss. His brother reports a similar two-week episode at 19 during a period of heavy use that resolved. Which reasoning is strongest across the timeline, developmental and formulation skills of this level?
questions.answer: Record the timeline of job loss, symptom onset, use and last use; keep a substance-related explanation and a condition persisting outside use as competing hypotheses; and state the reassessment after abstinence that would discriminate between them, while not treating the history as settled
questions.distractor: A substance-induced psychosis is the explanation, because both episodes occurred during heavy use and the pattern therefore resolves with abstinence
questions.correction: The association is consistent with a substance-related contribution but the earlier episode and the onset before use mean the substance cannot account for the whole picture. Order of onset is evidence rather than proof, and the discriminating observation is course during sustained abstinence.

questions.prompt: A fictional department proposes a quality dashboard built from four indicators: mean symptom score, number of risk assessments completed with a stratified band, mean therapist-rated improvement, and percentage of cases closed within twelve weeks. Using the reasoning of this level, which answer best describes the problem?
questions.answer: Every indicator measures a proxy the level has shown to be unreliable or incomplete: symptoms are not the recovery target, bands cannot predict, therapist-rated change is unblinded, and case closure can mean withdrawal of the supports a person's goals require
questions.distractor: The dashboard is reasonable but should add a fifth indicator for adverse events and physical health monitoring to be comprehensive
questions.correction: Adding an indicator would improve the dashboard without fixing the four. Each existing measure omits or distorts the thing it is taken to represent, and the effect of measuring them is to optimise the service for bands, ratings and closures rather than for needs, safety and the goals people set for themselves.
